3.34 Strong Interview Explanation

You can explain RDS creation like:

Creating an RDS instance involves provisioning managed database infrastructure inside a VPC. During setup we configure the database engine, instance class, storage type, networking, subnet groups, security groups, backups, monitoring, encryption, and optional high availability settings like Multi-AZ. AWS then provisions compute, storage, endpoint DNS, monitoring, and backup infrastructure automatically.
RDS Networking

4. RDS Networking

RDS networking is one of the MOST important production topics.

Most real-world RDS problems are actually:

  • networking problems
  • security group problems
  • routing problems
  • DNS problems

NOT PostgreSQL problems.

If you deeply understand RDS networking:

  • production becomes easier
  • debugging becomes easier
  • interviews become much easier

4.1 High-Level Networking Architecture

RDS exists inside AWS networking infrastructure.

Main components:

Internet
   ↓
VPC
   ↓
Subnets
   ↓
Route Tables
   ↓
Security Groups
   ↓
RDS

Important:

RDS is NOT publicly floating on internet by default.

It exists inside AWS networking boundaries.

4.2 VPC (Virtual Private Cloud)

Every RDS instance exists inside a:

Amazon Web Services VPC.

A VPC is basically:

Private isolated AWS network

Think of it like:

  • your private cloud network
  • your internal datacenter

Inside VPC you place:

  • EC2
  • RDS
  • Load Balancers
  • Lambda ENIs
  • ECS containers

4.3 Why VPC Matters

VPC controls:

  • isolation
  • internal communication
  • routing
  • internet access
  • security boundaries

Example:

VPC A
 ├── Backend EC2
 └── RDS PostgreSQL

Backend and DB communicate internally.

4.4 Subnets

Subnets divide VPC into smaller networks.

Example:

VPC 10.0.0.0/16

├── Public Subnet
│     10.0.1.0/24
│
└── Private Subnet
      10.0.2.0/24

Resources are placed inside subnets.

4.5 Public Subnet

A public subnet has:

Route to Internet Gateway

Meaning:

  • internet traffic allowed

Usually used for:

  • Load Balancers
  • Bastion hosts
  • public EC2 servers

4.6 Private Subnet

Private subnet has NO direct internet access.

Usually used for:

  • databases
  • internal services
  • backend infrastructure

Production RDS should usually be:

Inside private subnet

4.7 Real Production Architecture

Typical architecture:

Internet
   ↓
Load Balancer (Public)
   ↓
Backend EC2 (Private)
   ↓
RDS PostgreSQL (Private)

This is extremely common in production.

4.8 Why Private RDS is Important

If DB becomes public:

  • internet scanners can find it
  • brute force attacks possible
  • attack surface increases

Even with strong password:

  • exposure is dangerous

Best practice:

Never expose production DB publicly.

4.9 Internet Gateway (IGW)

Internet Gateway allows:

  • inbound internet traffic
  • outbound internet traffic

Public subnet route table usually contains:

0.0.0.0/0 → IGW

Meaning:

  • all unknown traffic goes to internet

4.10 NAT Gateway

Private resources sometimes need outbound internet.

Example:

  • downloading updates
  • external APIs

But we still do NOT want inbound internet access.

Solution:

NAT Gateway

Flow:

Private EC2
    ↓
NAT Gateway
    ↓
Internet

Important:

NAT allows outbound only.

4.11 DB Subnet Groups

RDS requires:

DB Subnet Group

This is:

  • collection of subnets
  • usually across AZs

Example:

Subnet Group
 ├── subnet-us-east-1a
 └── subnet-us-east-1b

Why?

Because RDS supports:

  • failover
  • Multi-AZ deployment

4.12 Why Multiple AZs Matter

If one Availability Zone fails:

AZ-1 fails
   ↓
RDS can move to AZ-2

Without multiple subnets:

  • failover impossible

4.13 Publicly Accessible Setting

During RDS creation AWS asks:

Publicly Accessible?

This setting is VERY misunderstood.

Publicly Accessible = YES

AWS assigns:

  • public DNS resolution
  • public routing capability

If Security Group also allows:

Your laptop
   ↓
Internet
   ↓
RDS

Possible.

Publicly Accessible = NO

No direct internet route.

Only internal VPC resources can connect.

Example:

EC2 Backend
   ↓
Private RDS

4.14 Security Groups

Security Groups are virtual firewalls.

Attached directly to:

  • RDS
  • EC2
  • Load Balancers

Example:

Allow TCP 5432
from backend SG

4.15 Important Security Group Concept

Security Groups are:

STATEFUL

Meaning:

  • return traffic automatically allowed

You allow:

  • inbound request

AWS automatically handles:

  • response traffic

4.16 Security Group Example

Production example:

RDS SG:
Allow 5432
Source:
Backend-EC2-SG

NOT:

0.0.0.0/0

because that means:

Entire internet can attempt DB connection.

4.17 NACLs (Network ACLs)

NACLs operate at:

Subnet level

Characteristics:

  • stateless
  • allow + deny rules

Less commonly modified than SGs.

4.18 Stateful vs Stateless

FeatureSecurity GroupNACL
LevelResourceSubnet
StatefulYesNo
Deny rulesNoYes
Easier managementYesHarder

4.19 RDS Endpoint

RDS uses DNS endpoint.

Example:

mydb.abc123.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com

Applications connect using:

  • hostname
  • NOT IP

4.20 Why DNS Endpoint Matters

AWS may:

  • replace hardware
  • failover DB
  • migrate infrastructure

If applications used raw IPs:

  • infrastructure changes break app

Instead:

DNS stays same
while infrastructure changes behind it.

VERY important cloud concept.

4.21 Internal vs External Connectivity

Internal Connectivity

Example:

Backend EC2
    ↓
Private RDS

Uses:

  • private AWS networking
  • internal IPs

Fast and secure.

External Connectivity

Example:

Laptop
   ↓
Internet
   ↓
Public RDS

Usually temporary:

  • development
  • admin access

Not ideal for production.

4.22 Bastion Host Architecture

Production admins often connect through:

Bastion Host

Architecture:

Laptop
   ↓
Bastion EC2
   ↓
Private RDS

This avoids exposing DB publicly.

4.23 VPN Architecture

Large companies often use:

VPN → VPC → Private RDS

Developers first connect to VPN.

Then access internal DB.

Very common enterprise architecture.

4.24 RDS and EC2 Communication

Most common architecture:

Backend EC2
     ↓
RDS

Requirements:

  • same VPC or peered VPC
  • SG rules
  • correct routing
  • correct DNS

4.25 Cross-VPC Access

Possible using:

  • VPC Peering
  • Transit Gateway
  • PrivateLink

Advanced architectures.

4.26 Common Networking Problems

Most common:

1. Security Group Blocking

Example:

Timeout connection

because:

  • port 5432 blocked

2. Public Access Disabled

Laptop cannot connect because:

  • DB private

3. Wrong VPC

EC2 and RDS in different isolated VPCs.

4. Wrong Route Table

Traffic cannot reach target subnet.

5. DNS Resolution Failure

Endpoint cannot resolve.

4.27 Debugging Flow

When connection fails:

Check in order:

1. Is DB available?
2. Correct endpoint?
3. Correct port?
4. Correct SG?
5. Public/private issue?
6. Same VPC?
7. Route tables?
8. DNS resolution?
9. NACL issue?
10. Authentication issue?

This order is VERY important.

4.28 Mental Model

Think of RDS networking like:

Internet Layer
    ↓
VPC Layer
    ↓
Subnet Layer
    ↓
Security Layer
    ↓
RDS Instance

Each layer controls access.

4.29 Strong Production Insight

Most beginners think:

Database problem

But actually many failures are:

Networking problem

Especially:

  • SG misconfigurations
  • wrong subnet
  • private/public confusion
  • routing problems

4.30 Strong Interview Explanation

You can explain RDS networking like:

RDS networking is built inside a VPC using subnet groups, security groups, route tables, and optional public accessibility settings. Production RDS deployments are usually private and accessible only through internal services such as EC2 backends or VPN-connected environments. Security Groups control resource-level access while subnet groups provide multi-AZ placement for failover and availability. Applications connect using DNS endpoints instead of fixed IP addresses because AWS may change underlying infrastructure during failover or maintenance.
RDS Security

5. RDS Security

RDS security is one of the MOST important production topics.

Because your database contains:

  • users
  • passwords
  • payments
  • business data
  • tokens
  • transactions
  • personal information

A compromised database can destroy an entire system.

In production:

Database security
=
business security

5.1 Security Layers in RDS

RDS security is NOT one thing.

It consists of multiple layers:

1. Network Security
2. Authentication
3. Authorization
4. Encryption
5. Monitoring/Auditing
6. Backup Protection
7. Infrastructure Isolation

Very important concept:

Security is layered.

5.2 Shared Responsibility Model

AWS and you both share security responsibilities.

AWS Responsibilities

AWS secures:

  • physical servers
  • AWS datacenters
  • storage hardware
  • networking infrastructure
  • hypervisor
  • managed infrastructure

Your Responsibilities

You secure:

  • DB credentials
  • SQL permissions
  • application access
  • security groups
  • query safety
  • sensitive data
  • backups
  • users/roles

Important:

AWS securing infrastructure
does NOT mean your DB is automatically secure.

5.3 Main Security Components

Core RDS security systems:

- Security Groups
- Private Subnets
- IAM
- DB Authentication
- Encryption
- SSL/TLS
- KMS
- Secrets Manager
- Monitoring/Auditing

5.4 Security Groups

Security Groups are the FIRST line of defense.

They act like:

  • virtual firewalls

Example:

Allow:
TCP 5432
FROM:
Backend EC2 SG

Meaning:

  • only backend servers can connect

5.5 Dangerous Security Group Mistake

VERY common beginner mistake:

0.0.0.0/0

on PostgreSQL port 5432.

This means:

Entire internet
can attempt connection.

This is dangerous.

Even with strong passwords:

  • scanners
  • brute-force attacks
  • bot attacks

can target DB.

5.6 Production Security Group Architecture

Best practice:

Internet
   ↓
Load Balancer
   ↓
Backend EC2
   ↓
Private RDS

RDS SG:

Allow PostgreSQL ONLY
from backend EC2 SG

NOT from internet.

5.7 Public vs Private RDS

Public RDS

Can potentially be reached from internet.

Useful for:

  • temporary development
  • admin testing

Dangerous for:

  • production

Private RDS

No direct internet access.

Only internal AWS resources can connect.

Production best practice:

Use Private RDS

5.8 Authentication

Authentication means:

Who are you?

RDS supports:

  • username/password
  • IAM authentication

5.9 Standard Database Authentication

Most common.

Example:

username: postgres
password: ********

Applications connect using credentials.

Example:

DB_USER=postgres
DB_PASSWORD=supersecret

5.10 Strong Password Requirements

Weak passwords are dangerous.

Bad:

postgres123

Good:

  • long
  • random
  • unique

Example:

G7!vX92#kLm@qP

5.11 IAM Database Authentication

Advanced feature.

Instead of static password:

  • temporary auth token used

Benefits:

  • short-lived credentials
  • better security
  • centralized access management

Less common in small projects.

More common in enterprise systems.

5.12 Authorization

Authorization means:

What are you allowed to do?

Inside PostgreSQL you still manage:

  • roles
  • grants
  • permissions

Example:

GRANT SELECT ON users TO readonly_user;

RDS does NOT replace database permissions.

5.13 Principle of Least Privilege

One of the MOST important security concepts.

Meaning:

Give minimum permissions necessary.

Example:

Bad:

Backend uses superadmin DB user.

Better:

Backend uses restricted application user.

5.14 Encryption at Rest

Encryption at rest means:

Data stored on disk is encrypted.

RDS supports encryption using:

Amazon Web Services KMS.

Encrypted:

  • storage
  • backups
  • snapshots
  • replicas

5.15 KMS (Key Management Service)

KMS manages encryption keys.

Flow:

Data
   ↓
Encrypted using KMS key
   ↓
Stored securely

Benefits:

  • protection against stolen disks
  • compliance requirements
  • enterprise security

5.16 Encryption in Transit

Encryption in transit means:

Traffic between app and DB is encrypted.

Without encryption:

Network sniffing possible.

With encryption:

  • traffic protected
  • credentials protected
  • queries protected

5.17 SSL/TLS Connections

Applications can connect using SSL/TLS.

Example:

Backend
   ↓ TLS
RDS PostgreSQL

Important for:

  • production
  • public networks
  • compliance

5.18 SSL Certificate Validation

Applications may validate:

  • AWS certificate
  • trusted CA

Prevents:

  • MITM attacks
  • fake DB endpoints

5.19 Secrets Management

Hardcoding passwords is dangerous.

Bad:

password: "mypassword123"

Better:

  • environment variables
  • Secrets Manager

5.20 AWS Secrets Manager

Stores:

  • credentials
  • secrets
  • tokens

Benefits:

  • centralized management
  • secret rotation
  • auditability

Example:

Backend
   ↓
Secrets Manager
   ↓
Get DB credentials

5.21 Credential Rotation

Good production practice:

Change passwords periodically.

Reduces risk of:

  • leaked credentials
  • long-term compromise

5.22 Backup Security

Backups are sensitive.

Because backups contain:

  • full database
  • user data
  • passwords
  • transactions

RDS supports:

  • encrypted snapshots
  • protected backups

5.23 Snapshot Risks

If snapshots are exposed:

  • attacker may restore full DB

Important:

  • protect snapshot permissions
  • avoid public snapshots

5.24 Monitoring and Auditing

Security also requires visibility.

Monitor:

  • failed logins
  • suspicious queries
  • unusual traffic
  • connection spikes

5.25 CloudWatch Security Monitoring

CloudWatch can monitor:

  • CPU spikes
  • connection count
  • unusual behavior

Helps detect:

  • attacks
  • abuse
  • overload

5.26 Database Logs

Logs may contain:

  • authentication failures
  • errors
  • slow queries

Useful for:

  • debugging
  • security investigation

5.27 Network Isolation

Best production pattern:

Private RDS
inside private subnet

This drastically reduces exposure.

5.28 Bastion Host Architecture

Instead of public DB:

Laptop
   ↓
Bastion EC2
   ↓
Private RDS

Admins connect through bastion.

Much safer.

5.29 VPN Architecture

Enterprise systems often use:

VPN
   ↓
Private VPC
   ↓
Private RDS

Only VPN-connected developers can access DB.

5.30 Common Security Mistakes

1. Public Database

Most common beginner mistake.

2. Weak Passwords

Easy brute-force target.

3. Using Master User Everywhere

Dangerous.

4. No SSL

Traffic exposed.

5. Hardcoded Credentials

Secrets leak risk.

6. No Backup Encryption

Sensitive data exposed.

5.31 Production Security Architecture

Typical secure setup:

Internet
   ↓
CloudFront
   ↓
Load Balancer
   ↓
Backend EC2
   ↓
Private RDS

Additional protections:

- SG restrictions
- encryption
- TLS
- monitoring
- backups
- IAM
- Secrets Manager

5.32 Mental Model

Think of RDS security like:

Network Security
      ↓
Authentication
      ↓
Authorization
      ↓
Encryption
      ↓
Monitoring
      ↓
Backup Protection

Security is layered.

5.33 Real Production Insight

Most database breaches happen because of:

  • misconfiguration
  • exposed credentials
  • public access
  • weak permissions

NOT because PostgreSQL itself is weak.

5.34 Strong Interview Explanation

You can explain RDS security like:

RDS security is built using layered protection mechanisms including VPC isolation, private subnets, Security Groups, authentication, encryption at rest using KMS, TLS encryption in transit, IAM integration, Secrets Manager, and monitoring/auditing systems. In production architectures, RDS databases are typically private and accessible only from internal services such as backend EC2 instances or VPN-connected environments.
Connecting Applications to RDS

6. Connecting Applications to RDS

This is where your backend actually starts using RDS.

In production:

Frontend
    ↓
Backend API
    ↓
RDS PostgreSQL

Applications NEVER “talk” to storage directly.

They connect through:

  • TCP connection
  • database protocol
  • RDS endpoint
  • authentication

This section is VERY important because:

  • most beginner problems happen here
  • production bottlenecks happen here
  • scaling problems happen here
  • debugging usually starts here

6.1 High-Level Connection Flow

Example architecture:

Node.js Backend
      ↓
DNS Resolution
      ↓
RDS Endpoint
      ↓
TCP Connection
      ↓
PostgreSQL Authentication
      ↓
SQL Queries

6.2 RDS Endpoint

When RDS is created, AWS generates endpoint.

Example:

mydb.abc123.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com

Applications connect using:

  • hostname
  • username
  • password
  • database name
  • port

6.3 Why Endpoint Matters

Applications SHOULD NOT use raw IPs.

Because AWS may:

  • failover
  • replace hardware
  • migrate infrastructure

DNS endpoint remains stable.

Application
     ↓
Stable DNS Endpoint
     ↓
AWS changes infrastructure internally

VERY important cloud concept.

6.4 PostgreSQL Connection Components

To connect PostgreSQL app needs:

ComponentExample
Hostmydb.xxxx.rds.amazonaws.com
Port5432
Usernamepostgres
Passwordsecret
Databaseunipos

6.5 Default Ports

DatabasePort
PostgreSQL5432
MySQL3306
SQL Server1433

6.6 Local Machine Connection

You can connect from:

  • pgAdmin
  • DBeaver
  • psql
  • VSCode extensions

Requirements:

  • RDS publicly accessible OR VPN/Bastion
  • correct Security Group
  • correct credentials

6.7 Example pgAdmin Connection

Fields:

Host:
mydb.xxxx.rds.amazonaws.com

Port:
5432

Username:
postgres

Password:
********

If successful:

pgAdmin
   ↓
Internet/VPN
   ↓
RDS

6.8 Backend Connection

Most common architecture:

Frontend
   ↓
Backend API
   ↓
RDS

Backend acts as intermediary.

Clients should NEVER connect directly to DB.

6.9 Why Frontend Should Not Connect Directly

Bad architecture:

React Frontend
      ↓
RDS

Problems:

  • DB credentials exposed
  • security disaster
  • no business logic layer
  • SQL injection risks
  • impossible access control

Correct architecture:

Frontend
   ↓
Backend API
   ↓
RDS

6.10 Node.js PostgreSQL Connection

Most Node.js apps use:

  • pg
  • Prisma
  • Sequelize
  • TypeORM
  • Drizzle

Basic pg example:

import pg from "pg";

const pool = new pg.Pool({
  host: process.env.DB_HOST,
  port: 5432,
  user: process.env.DB_USER,
  password: process.env.DB_PASSWORD,
  database: process.env.DB_NAME,
});

6.11 Environment Variables

Credentials should NOT be hardcoded.

Bad:

password: "mypassword123"

Good:

DB_HOST=mydb.xxxx.rds.amazonaws.com
DB_USER=postgres
DB_PASSWORD=supersecret
DB_NAME=unipos

6.12 Connection Lifecycle

Connection flow:

1. Resolve DNS
2. Open TCP connection
3. Authenticate user
4. Create session
5. Execute queries
6. Return results
7. Close/reuse connection

6.13 TCP Connection

Database communication happens over TCP.

Example:

Backend
   ↓ TCP:5432
RDS PostgreSQL

6.14 DNS Resolution

Before connecting:

mydb.xxxx.rds.amazonaws.com

must resolve to IP.

DNS failure causes:

getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND

Very common error.

6.15 Authentication Phase

After TCP connection:

PostgreSQL validates:

  • username
  • password
  • permissions

If wrong:

password authentication failed

6.16 Database Sessions

Each connection creates:

  • DB session
  • memory usage
  • backend process/thread

Too many sessions can overload DB.

VERY important production concept.

6.17 Connection Pooling

One of the MOST important backend topics.

Without pooling:

Every request
creates new DB connection.

This is expensive.

6.18 Why New Connections Are Expensive

Creating DB connection requires:

  • TCP handshake
  • authentication
  • memory allocation
  • DB session creation

Doing this per request is inefficient.

6.19 Connection Pool

Pool reuses existing connections.

Architecture:

Backend Requests
      ↓
Connection Pool
      ↓
Few reusable DB connections
      ↓
RDS

VERY important for scalability.

6.20 Pool Example

const pool = new Pool({
  max: 20
});

Meaning:

  • maximum 20 active DB connections

6.21 Why Pooling Matters

Without pooling:

  • DB crashes under traffic
  • connection exhaustion
  • latency spikes

With pooling:

  • stable connections
  • better scalability
  • lower overhead

6.22 RDS Connection Limits

Every RDS instance has:

  • max connections

Depends on:

  • RAM
  • instance class
  • engine

Example:

db.t3.micro
has much fewer max connections
than
db.r6g.large

6.23 Connection Exhaustion

Common production issue.

Example:

remaining connection slots are reserved

Causes:

  • too many clients
  • leaked connections
  • no pooling

6.24 Connection Leak

Dangerous bug.

Example:

const client = await pool.connect();

but never released.

Eventually:

  • all connections consumed
  • app stops working

6.25 Correct Pool Usage

Example:

const client = await pool.connect();

try {
  await client.query(...);
} finally {
  client.release();
}

VERY important.

6.26 SSL/TLS Connections

Production systems often use encrypted DB traffic.

Architecture:

Backend
   ↓ TLS
RDS

Protects:

  • credentials
  • queries
  • results

6.27 SSL Example

ssl: {
  rejectUnauthorized: false
}

Production systems may validate certificates more strictly.

6.28 Private RDS Connection

Most production systems use:

Backend EC2
    ↓
Private RDS

No internet exposure.

6.29 Public RDS Connection

Learning/dev setup:

Laptop
   ↓
Internet
   ↓
Public RDS

Useful temporarily.

Dangerous for production.

6.30 Bastion Host Access

Production admin access:

Laptop
   ↓
Bastion Host
   ↓
Private RDS

Safer architecture.

6.31 VPN Architecture

Enterprise systems often use:

Developer
   ↓ VPN
Private VPC
   ↓
Private RDS

6.32 ORMs and RDS

RDS works with:

  • Prisma
  • Sequelize
  • TypeORM
  • Drizzle
  • Knex

RDS does NOT care which ORM you use.

It only sees:

  • PostgreSQL/MySQL protocol traffic

6.33 Migrations

Applications often run:

  • migrations
  • schema updates

Example:

Backend startup
   ↓
Run migrations
   ↓
Use DB

6.34 Read/Write Flow

Typical architecture:

Writes
   ↓
Primary RDS

Reads
   ↓
Read Replica

Scaling concept.

6.35 Common Connection Errors

1. Security Group Blocking

Example:

Connection timeout

because:

  • port 5432 blocked

2. Wrong Credentials

password authentication failed

3. DNS Failure

ENOTFOUND

4. DB Not Public

Laptop cannot access private RDS.

5. Too Many Connections

remaining connection slots reserved

6.36 Debugging Flow

When DB connection fails:

Check in order:

1. Is RDS available?
2. Correct endpoint?
3. Correct port?
4. SG allows access?
5. Public/private issue?
6. Correct credentials?
7. DNS working?
8. Connection limit reached?
9. SSL issue?

VERY important production flow.

6.37 Real Production Architecture

Common architecture:

Users
   ↓
CloudFront
   ↓
Load Balancer
   ↓
Backend EC2/ECS
   ↓
Connection Pool
   ↓
Private RDS

6.38 Mental Model

Think of app connection flow like:

Application
    ↓
Connection Pool
    ↓
DNS Endpoint
    ↓
TCP Connection
    ↓
Authentication
    ↓
RDS Session
    ↓
SQL Queries

6.39 Real Production Insight

Many production outages are NOT:

  • PostgreSQL crashes

They are:

  • exhausted connections
  • leaked sessions
  • missing pooling
  • SG mistakes
  • DNS issues

Connection management is extremely important.

6.40 Strong Interview Explanation

You can explain application connection flow like:

Applications connect to RDS using the database engine protocol over TCP through an AWS-generated DNS endpoint. The application provides host, port, credentials, and database name to establish authenticated sessions. Production systems usually connect from backend services inside the same VPC using private networking and connection pooling to efficiently reuse database connections and avoid connection exhaustion.
Storage in RDS

7. Storage in RDS

Storage is where ALL actual database data lives.

This includes:

  • tables
  • rows
  • indexes
  • WAL logs
  • transactions
  • backups
  • snapshots

A database without storage is useless.

In production:

Most database performance
depends heavily on storage performance.

NOT only CPU.

7.1 High-Level Storage Architecture

RDS storage architecture:

Application
    ↓
DB Engine
    ↓
Compute Instance
    ↓
Managed Storage Layer

Important:

Compute and storage are separate.

This is a VERY important cloud concept.

7.2 Compute vs Storage Separation

In traditional servers:

CPU + RAM + Disk
inside same physical machine

In cloud systems:

Compute
   ≠
Storage

AWS can:

  • resize compute separately
  • resize storage separately

Example:

Increase RAM
without changing storage

or:

Increase storage
without changing CPU

Very important architecture concept.

7.3 What RDS Storage Contains

Storage holds:

- tables
- indexes
- transaction logs
- WAL files
- metadata
- temporary files
- backups

7.4 Persistent Storage

RDS storage is:

Persistent

Meaning:

  • survives reboot
  • survives restart
  • survives maintenance

Unlike temporary memory.

7.5 Database Writes

When application inserts data:

Backend
   ↓
RDS Engine
   ↓
Write to Storage

Example:

INSERT INTO users(name)
VALUES('John');

Eventually persisted to storage.

7.6 Reads vs Writes

Storage workload has two main operations:

OperationMeaning
ReadFetch data
WriteStore/update data

Example:

SELECT * FROM users;

→ Read operation

UPDATE users SET name='Mike';

→ Write operation

7.7 Storage Performance Matters

Slow storage causes:

  • slow queries
  • high latency
  • replication lag
  • application slowness

Important:

Database performance
is often storage-bound.

NOT CPU-bound.

7.8 Storage Types in RDS

RDS supports multiple storage types.

Main ones:

Storage TypeUsage
gp2Older SSD
gp3Modern SSD
io1/io2High-performance enterprise

7.9 gp2 Storage

Older SSD storage.

Characteristics:

  • decent performance
  • burst model
  • older generation

Still works but newer systems usually prefer:

gp3

7.10 gp3 Storage

Modern recommended storage type.

Advantages:

  • cheaper
  • configurable performance
  • independent scaling
  • more flexible

Production recommendation:

Use gp3 in most cases

7.11 Provisioned IOPS Storage

Types:

  • io1
  • io2

Used for:

  • extremely high throughput
  • enterprise workloads
  • heavy transaction systems

Examples:

  • banking
  • fintech
  • enterprise ERP

7.12 What are IOPS?

IOPS means:

Input/Output Operations Per Second

Measures:

  • disk speed capability

Higher IOPS:

  • faster reads/writes
  • lower latency

7.13 Storage Latency

Latency means:

How long storage takes
to respond.

Lower latency:

  • better performance

High latency causes:

  • slow APIs
  • slow queries
  • timeouts

7.14 Throughput

Throughput means:

Amount of data transferred per second.

Examples:

  • MB/s
  • GB/s

Important for:

  • analytics
  • backups
  • large queries

7.15 Allocated Storage

When creating RDS you specify:

Allocated Storage

Example:

20 GB

This means:

  • initial disk size

7.16 Running Out of Storage

VERY dangerous production issue.

If storage becomes full:

Database may stop writes

Possible consequences:

  • failed transactions
  • app outages
  • crashes

7.17 Storage Autoscaling

RDS can automatically increase storage.

Example:

20 GB
   ↓
40 GB automatically

Very useful in production.

Prevents:

  • outages from full disk

7.18 Why Autoscaling Matters

Traffic growth is unpredictable.

Example:

Application suddenly grows

More:

  • users
  • logs
  • transactions
  • files

Storage consumption increases rapidly.

Autoscaling protects system.

7.19 Storage Encryption

RDS supports encrypted storage using:

Amazon Web Services KMS.

Encrypted:

  • storage volumes
  • snapshots
  • backups
  • replicas

7.20 Storage Replication

In Multi-AZ:

Primary Storage
      ↓
Synchronous replication
      ↓
Standby Storage

This improves:

  • durability
  • availability

7.21 WAL Logs (PostgreSQL)

PostgreSQL uses:

WAL = Write Ahead Log

VERY important concept.

Before modifying actual table:

  • change written to WAL first

Purpose:

  • crash recovery
  • replication
  • consistency

7.22 WAL Flow

PostgreSQL write process:

Application
    ↓
WAL log
    ↓
Actual table storage

This guarantees durability.

7.23 Why WAL Matters

If DB crashes:

PostgreSQL can replay WAL

to recover transactions.

WAL also used for:

  • replication
  • backups
  • PITR

VERY important PostgreSQL concept.

7.24 Temporary Files

Queries may create temporary storage.

Example:

  • sorting huge datasets
  • joins
  • aggregations

Large temp usage can slow DB.

7.25 Index Storage

Indexes are stored separately on disk.

Indexes improve:

  • query speed

But indexes also:

  • consume storage
  • increase write cost

Tradeoff important.

7.26 Backup Storage

Automated backups stored separately.

RDS can:

  • snapshot storage
  • restore storage state

7.27 Snapshots

Snapshots are storage-level backups.

Can restore:

  • exact DB state

Example:

Snapshot:
2026-05-12

Used for:

  • disaster recovery
  • cloning
  • migrations

7.28 Point-In-Time Recovery (PITR)

Uses:

  • snapshots
  • WAL logs

Allows:

Restore DB
to exact timestamp

Example:

Restore:
2026-05-12 14:20:31

Very powerful feature.

7.29 Storage and Performance

Performance depends heavily on:

  • IOPS
  • throughput
  • latency
  • storage type

Bad storage:

  • bottlenecks entire DB

7.30 Read-Heavy Workloads

Example:

Analytics dashboard

Many reads:

  • storage read pressure increases

Possible solutions:

  • replicas
  • caching
  • faster storage

7.31 Write-Heavy Workloads

Example:

Financial transaction system

Many writes:

  • WAL pressure
  • replication pressure
  • disk sync pressure

Requires:

  • strong storage performance

7.32 SSD vs Magnetic Storage

Modern RDS mainly uses SSD.

SSD advantages:

  • lower latency
  • higher IOPS
  • better throughput

Magnetic storage mostly outdated.

7.33 Storage Monitoring

Important metrics:

  • free storage space
  • read IOPS
  • write IOPS
  • latency
  • throughput

Monitored using:

  • CloudWatch
  • Performance Insights

7.34 Common Storage Problems

1. Full Disk

Causes outages.

2. High Latency

Slow queries.

3. Low IOPS

Cannot handle workload.

4. Storage Bottlenecks

DB becomes slow despite good CPU.

5. Excessive WAL Growth

Can consume storage rapidly.

7.35 Real Production Insight

Most developers think:

CPU = DB performance

But often real bottleneck is:

Storage latency
or
IOPS

Especially:

  • large datasets
  • analytics
  • high write systems

7.36 Real Production Architecture

Storage architecture:

Application
    ↓
RDS Compute
    ↓
Managed SSD Storage
    ↓
Snapshots/WAL
    ↓
Replication

7.37 Mental Model

Think of RDS storage like:

Compute
   ↓
Database Engine
   ↓
Persistent SSD Storage
   ↓
Backups + WAL + Snapshots

Storage is the durability layer.

7.38 Strong Interview Explanation

You can explain RDS storage like:

RDS storage is a managed persistent storage layer attached to the database compute instance. It stores tables, indexes, WAL logs, snapshots, and transaction data. AWS provides multiple storage types such as gp3 and provisioned IOPS storage, allowing different performance profiles based on workload requirements. Storage can scale independently from compute and supports encryption, automated backups, replication, and point-in-time recovery capabilities.
High Availability

8. High Availability in RDS

High Availability (HA) means:

Keeping database available
even when failures happen.

Failures WILL happen in production:

  • server crashes
  • disk failures
  • AZ failures
  • hardware issues
  • networking issues
  • maintenance events

HA exists to reduce:

  • downtime
  • outages
  • data loss

8.1 What is Downtime?

Downtime means:

Application cannot use database.

Consequences:

  • APIs fail
  • users cannot login
  • payments fail
  • transactions fail

For production businesses:

Database downtime
=
business downtime

8.2 Single Point of Failure (SPOF)

One of the MOST important concepts.

Example bad architecture:

Backend
   ↓
Single PostgreSQL Server

If that DB crashes:

Entire system goes down.

This is:

  • Single Point of Failure

HA tries to remove SPOFs.

8.3 High Availability Goal

Goal:

System survives failures
with minimal downtime.

Important:

  • HA is NOT zero failures
  • HA is surviving failures

8.4 Availability Zones (AZs)

AWS regions contain multiple AZs.

Example:

us-east-1a
us-east-1b
us-east-1c

Each AZ is:

  • separate datacenter infrastructure
  • isolated power/networking

Important concept:

AZ failure should not destroy system.

8.5 Multi-AZ

Main RDS HA feature:

Multi-AZ Deployment

Purpose:

High Availability

NOT read scaling.

VERY important distinction.

8.6 Single-AZ Architecture

Without HA:

Primary DB
   ↓
Single storage

Failure causes:

  • outage
  • downtime

8.7 Multi-AZ Architecture

With Multi-AZ:

Primary DB (AZ-1)
        ↓
Synchronous Replication
        ↓
Standby DB (AZ-2)

Now:

  • standby copy exists
  • automatic failover possible

8.8 Standby Instance

Standby is:

  • passive replica
  • not used for reads normally

Purpose:

  • failover only

Important:

Multi-AZ standby
is NOT read replica.

8.9 Synchronous Replication

One of the MOST important concepts.

Flow:

Write request
      ↓
Primary DB
      ↓
Standby DB receives write
      ↓
Commit success

Meaning:

Both DBs stay consistent.

8.10 Why Synchronous Replication Matters

If primary crashes:

Standby already has latest data.

Very low data loss risk.

8.11 Failover

Failover means:

Switching from failed primary
to standby instance.

Flow:

Primary crashes
      ↓
AWS detects failure
      ↓
Standby promoted
      ↓
DNS endpoint redirected
      ↓
Application reconnects

Automatic process.

8.12 Automatic Failover

RDS can automatically failover during:

  • hardware failure
  • storage failure
  • AZ failure
  • maintenance events

Very important production feature.

8.13 DNS Endpoint During Failover

Applications connect using:

mydb.xxxx.rds.amazonaws.com

NOT raw IP.

Why important?

Because during failover:

AWS changes infrastructure
behind same DNS endpoint.

Applications reconnect automatically.

8.14 Failover Downtime

Failover is NOT instant.

Usually:

  • seconds
  • sometimes 1–2 minutes

During failover:

  • temporary DB unavailability

Applications should handle:

  • retries
  • reconnect logic

8.15 Application Retry Logic

Production backends should support:

Reconnect after temporary DB failure

Because failovers happen.

Without retry logic:

  • application crashes

8.16 Multi-AZ Storage Replication

Storage also replicated.

Architecture:

Primary Storage
      ↓
Synchronous replication
      ↓
Standby Storage

Improves:

  • durability
  • resilience

8.17 Why Multi-AZ Costs More

AWS runs:

  • second DB instance
  • second storage
  • replication infrastructure

So cost roughly increases significantly.

Tradeoff:

Higher cost
=
Higher availability

8.18 Multi-AZ vs Read Replica

VERY important interview question.

FeatureMulti-AZRead Replica
PurposeHigh AvailabilityRead Scaling
ReadableNoYes
ReplicationSynchronousAsynchronous
FailoverAutomaticUsually manual promotion
Data consistencyStrongPotential lag

8.19 Read Replica ≠ HA

Many beginners misunderstand this.

Read replicas mainly solve:

Scaling reads

NOT:

  • guaranteed HA

8.20 Availability vs Durability

Important distinction.

Availability

Means:

Can users access DB?

Durability

Means:

Will data survive failure?

Multi-AZ improves BOTH.

8.21 Hardware Failures

Without HA:

Disk failure
    ↓
DB outage

With Multi-AZ:

Disk failure
    ↓
Failover to standby

System survives.

8.22 AZ Failure

Entire AZ may fail.

Without Multi-AZ:

  • DB unavailable

With Multi-AZ:

AZ-1 fails
    ↓
Standby in AZ-2 survives

VERY important cloud design principle.

8.23 Maintenance Events

AWS sometimes:

  • patches infrastructure
  • upgrades systems
  • replaces hardware

Without Multi-AZ:

  • more downtime

With Multi-AZ:

  • failover minimizes downtime

8.24 Detecting Failure

RDS monitors:

  • compute health
  • networking
  • storage
  • DB responsiveness

If unhealthy:

  • failover triggered

8.25 Application Perspective

Applications do NOT know:

  • which physical server running DB

They only know:

DNS endpoint

This abstraction is VERY important.

8.26 Real Production Architecture

Typical production HA setup:

Users
   ↓
Load Balancer
   ↓
Backend Cluster
   ↓
RDS Multi-AZ PostgreSQL

Optional:

  • replicas
  • monitoring
  • backups

8.27 Why HA Matters for Backend Systems

Imagine your POS/CRM:

Without HA:

Single DB crashes
    ↓
School/business stops working

With HA:

  • much lower outage risk

8.28 Common Misunderstandings

1. Multi-AZ improves reads

FALSE.

Standby not normally readable.

2. Read Replica replaces Multi-AZ

FALSE.

Different purpose.

3. HA means zero downtime

FALSE.

It means:

  • minimized downtime
  • automatic recovery

8.29 HA Tradeoffs

Benefits:

  • resilience
  • failover
  • reduced downtime

Costs:

  • more expensive
  • more complex
  • slightly higher write latency

8.30 Why Write Latency Slightly Increases

Because synchronous replication requires:

Primary waits for standby confirmation.

Extra network/storage step.

8.31 Disaster Recovery vs High Availability

Important distinction.

High Availability

Focus:

  • short-term failures
  • automatic recovery

Disaster Recovery

Focus:

  • catastrophic events
  • region loss
  • large-scale recovery

Different concepts.

8.32 Multi-Region vs Multi-AZ

Multi-AZ

Same region.

Example:

us-east-1a
us-east-1b

Multi-Region

Different regions.

Example:

us-east-1
eu-central-1

Much more complex.

8.33 Monitoring HA

Important metrics:

  • replication health
  • failover events
  • latency
  • DB status

Monitored via:

  • CloudWatch
  • RDS Events

8.34 Real Production Insight

Most companies care LESS about:

  • tiny performance gains

and MORE about:

Availability

Because outages are extremely expensive.

8.35 Mental Model

Think of HA like:

Primary DB
      ↓
Synchronous standby copy
      ↓
Automatic failover
      ↓
Same DNS endpoint

8.36 Strong Interview Explanation

You can explain RDS High Availability like:

RDS High Availability is commonly implemented using Multi-AZ deployments where AWS maintains a synchronous standby replica in another Availability Zone. If the primary database instance fails due to hardware, networking, storage, or AZ-level issues, AWS automatically promotes the standby instance and redirects the DNS endpoint to minimize downtime and preserve durability. Multi-AZ focuses on availability and failover rather than read scaling.
Read Replicas and Scaling

9. Read Replicas vs Scaling in RDS

This is one of the MOST important RDS topics for:

  • system design interviews
  • production backend systems
  • scalability architecture

Because eventually every successful application hits:

Database bottleneck

And many developers incorrectly think:

Just increase CPU forever

But scalable systems require:

  • proper scaling strategies
  • read distribution
  • replica architecture

9.1 First Important Concept

Databases usually become bottlenecks before backend servers.

Why?

Because:

  • backend can scale horizontally easily
  • database writes are harder to scale

Example:

100 backend servers
      ↓
1 database

Eventually DB becomes overloaded.

9.2 Two Main Scaling Types

Database scaling mainly has:

Scaling TypeMeaning
Vertical ScalingBigger server
Horizontal ScalingMore servers

9.3 Vertical Scaling

Vertical scaling means:

Increase power of existing DB instance

Example:

db.t3.micro
    ↓
db.m5.large

Increasing:

  • CPU
  • RAM
  • network performance

9.4 Advantages of Vertical Scaling

Benefits:

  • simple
  • fast
  • minimal architecture changes

Good for:

  • early-stage systems
  • moderate workloads

9.5 Problems with Vertical Scaling

Cannot scale forever.

Eventually:

  • hardware limits
  • cost explosion
  • downtime during resize
  • diminishing returns

Important:

Vertical scaling has limits.

9.6 Horizontal Scaling

Horizontal scaling means:

Add additional database servers

Usually:

  • replicas
  • distributed workloads

This is where:

Read Replicas

become important.

9.7 What is Read Replica?

A Read Replica is:

Copy of primary database
used for READ operations

Architecture:

Primary DB
      ↓
Asynchronous Replication
      ↓
Read Replica

9.8 Main Purpose of Read Replicas

Purpose:

Scale READ traffic

NOT:

  • primary HA mechanism
  • synchronous failover

VERY important.

9.9 Read vs Write Traffic

Applications perform:

  • reads
  • writes

Example:

SELECT * FROM users;

→ READ

INSERT INTO users VALUES(...);

→ WRITE

Most applications are:

Read-heavy

Meaning:

  • many more reads than writes

9.10 Why Reads Become Problem

Example:

100,000 users

All performing:

  • dashboards
  • feeds
  • searches
  • analytics
  • reports

DB becomes overloaded with reads.

9.11 Read Scaling Architecture

Instead of:

All traffic
    ↓
Single DB

Use:

Writes
   ↓
Primary DB

Reads
   ↓
Read Replicas

Now workload distributed.

9.12 Asynchronous Replication

Read replicas use:

Asynchronous replication

Meaning:

Primary commits write FIRST
then replica updates later.

Important consequence:

Replica may lag behind primary.

VERY important concept.

9.13 Replication Lag

Replication lag means:

Replica not fully updated yet.

Example:

User updates profile
     ↓
Immediately reads from replica
     ↓
Old data appears temporarily

This is eventual consistency behavior.

9.14 Why Lag Happens

Reasons:

  • heavy writes
  • network latency
  • replica overload
  • slow storage
  • large transactions

9.15 Eventual Consistency

Read replicas introduce:

Eventual consistency

Meaning:

  • replica eventually matches primary
  • but not instantly

9.16 Strong Consistency vs Eventual Consistency

TypeMeaning
Strong ConsistencyLatest data guaranteed
Eventual ConsistencyReplica catches up later

Primary DB:

  • strong consistency

Read Replica:

  • eventual consistency

9.17 Why Some Reads Should NOT Use Replicas

Critical operations may require latest data.

Examples:

  • payments
  • balances
  • financial systems

These should often read from:

  • primary DB

NOT replica.

9.18 Good Use Cases for Read Replicas

Excellent for:

  • analytics dashboards
  • reports
  • search pages
  • feeds
  • statistics
  • product listings

Because slight lag acceptable.

9.19 Multiple Read Replicas

Architecture:

Primary DB
   ├── Replica 1
   ├── Replica 2
   └── Replica 3

Traffic distributed across replicas.

9.20 Application Read Routing

Backend decides:

Writes → Primary
Reads → Replica

Application-level logic.

9.21 Example Architecture

Frontend
    ↓
Backend API
    ├── Writes → Primary DB
    └── Reads  → Read Replica

Very common production architecture.

9.22 Read Replica Promotion

Replica can sometimes be promoted:

Replica
   ↓
Standalone DB

Useful during:

  • migration
  • disaster recovery
  • failover scenarios

9.23 Read Replicas vs Multi-AZ

VERY important interview topic.

FeatureRead ReplicaMulti-AZ
PurposeRead ScalingHigh Availability
ReplicationAsynchronousSynchronous
ReadableYesNo
Lag possibleYesMinimal
Automatic failoverUsually NoYes

9.24 Multi-AZ is NOT Scaling

Multi-AZ improves:

  • resilience
  • failover

NOT:

  • query throughput
  • read scalability

Very important distinction.

9.25 Read Replicas are NOT True HA

Because:

  • asynchronous lag possible
  • promotion may be manual
  • not instant failover

Their main purpose:

Scale reads

9.26 Scaling Bottlenecks

Even with replicas:

  • writes still hit primary

Eventually primary may become bottleneck.

This becomes harder scaling problem.

9.27 Write Scaling is Hard

Relational DB writes require:

  • consistency
  • transactions
  • locks

Much harder than scaling reads.

This is why:

  • read scaling easier
  • write scaling harder

9.28 Scaling Strategy Evolution

Typical growth:

1. Single DB
      ↓
2. Bigger DB
      ↓
3. Add replicas
      ↓
4. Caching
      ↓
5. Sharding/distributed systems

9.29 Read Replicas and Analytics

Good pattern:

Production Primary
      ↓
Analytics Replica

Analytics queries avoid slowing production DB.

9.30 Heavy Queries Problem

Bad architecture:

Analytics queries
run on production primary

Can:

  • slow APIs
  • overload DB
  • cause latency spikes

Replicas isolate workload.

9.31 Replica Geography

Replicas may exist:

  • same AZ
  • different AZ
  • different region

Cross-region replicas help:

  • global apps
  • DR strategies

9.32 Cross-Region Replicas

Architecture:

us-east-1 Primary
       ↓
eu-central-1 Replica

Useful for:

  • global users
  • lower latency
  • DR

9.33 Replica Monitoring

Important metrics:

  • replication lag
  • replica CPU
  • throughput
  • connection count

Monitored using:

  • CloudWatch
  • Performance Insights

9.34 Common Read Replica Problems

1. Replication Lag

Most common issue.

2. Reads Returning Old Data

Due to asynchronous replication.

3. Replica Overload

Replica itself can become bottleneck.

4. Wrong Query Routing

Critical reads accidentally use replica.

9.35 Caching vs Read Replicas

Another important scaling concept.

Read Replica

Still queries DB.

Cache

Avoids DB entirely.

Example:

  • Redis
  • Memcached

Architecture:

Backend
   ↓
Redis Cache
   ↓
RDS

Very common scaling strategy.

9.36 Scaling Reality

Real production scaling usually combines:

- Bigger instance
- Read replicas
- Caching
- Query optimization
- Better indexes

NOT just one solution.

9.37 Query Optimization First

Many scaling problems are actually:

Bad SQL

NOT insufficient hardware.

Example:

SELECT * FROM huge_table;

without indexes.

Always optimize before scaling aggressively.

9.38 Real Production Architecture

Typical scalable architecture:

Users
   ↓
Load Balancer
   ↓
Backend Cluster
   ↓
Connection Pool
   ├── Writes → Primary DB
   └── Reads  → Read Replicas

9.39 Mental Model

Think like:

Primary DB
   ↓
Handles:
- writes
- critical reads

Replicas
   ↓
Handle:
- scalable reads
- analytics
- reports

9.40 Strong Interview Explanation

You can explain Read Replicas and scaling like:

RDS scaling can be achieved vertically by increasing instance resources or horizontally using Read Replicas. Read Replicas use asynchronous replication to create readable copies of the primary database, allowing read-heavy workloads to be distributed across multiple instances. They improve read scalability but do not provide the same guarantees as Multi-AZ deployments because replication lag may occur and consistency is eventual rather than fully synchronous.
Backups and Recovery

10. Backups and Recovery in RDS

Backups and recovery are one of the MOST important production topics.

Because eventually something WILL happen:

- accidental deletion
- bad deployment
- corrupted data
- dropped table
- ransomware
- failed migration
- human mistake
- infrastructure failure

Without backups:

Data may be permanently lost.

For real companies:

Database backups
=
business survival

10.1 Main Goal of Backups

Goal:

Restore database after failure.

Recovery should allow:

  • restoring data
  • restoring infrastructure
  • minimizing downtime
  • minimizing data loss

10.2 RDS Backup Types

RDS mainly provides:

Backup TypePurpose
Automated BackupsContinuous recovery
Manual SnapshotsLong-term restore points

10.3 Automated Backups

RDS automatically creates:

  • storage snapshots
  • transaction logs/WAL logs

Purpose:

  • automatic recovery
  • Point-In-Time Recovery (PITR)

AWS manages:

  • scheduling
  • storage
  • retention

10.4 How Automated Backups Work

Internally:

RDS Storage Snapshot
        +
Transaction Logs/WAL

Combined together:

  • allow exact recovery

10.5 Backup Retention Period

During RDS creation AWS asks:

Backup retention period

Example:

7 days

Meaning:

  • restore possible within last 7 days

10.6 Longer Retention

Longer retention:

  • more recovery flexibility
  • more storage cost

Example:

35 days retention

Common in production.

10.7 What Happens During Backup

AWS creates:

  • storage-level snapshot
  • transaction log capture

Usually without major downtime.

Important:

RDS backups are infrastructure-level operations.

NOT:

  • pg_dump style logical exports

10.8 Point-In-Time Recovery (PITR)

One of the MOST powerful RDS features.

Allows:

Restore database
to exact timestamp

Example:

Restore:
2026-05-12 14:20:31

VERY important production feature.

10.9 How PITR Works

Flow:

Base Snapshot
      +
WAL/Transaction Logs
      ↓
Replay changes
      ↓
Restore exact point

10.10 WAL Logs in PostgreSQL

PostgreSQL uses:

WAL = Write Ahead Log

Before modifying actual data:

  • change written to WAL first

WAL used for:

  • crash recovery
  • replication
  • PITR

VERY important PostgreSQL concept.

10.11 Example PITR Scenario

Imagine:

DROP TABLE users;

accidentally executed.

Without PITR:

  • disaster

With PITR:

Restore DB
to moment before DROP TABLE

Very powerful.

10.12 Manual Snapshots

Manual snapshots are:

  • user-triggered backups
  • retained until deleted

Unlike automated backups:

  • do not expire automatically

10.13 Snapshot Example

Example:

Before major migration

Create snapshot:

prod-before-migration

If migration fails:

  • restore snapshot

Very common production practice.

10.14 Automated Backup vs Snapshot

FeatureAutomated BackupManual Snapshot
AutomaticYesNo
ExpirationRetention-basedManual deletion
PITR supportYesNo
Long-term storageLimitedYes

10.15 Restoring Database

Restoration does NOT overwrite existing DB directly.

Instead:

AWS creates NEW RDS instance

Very important.

10.16 Restore Flow

Example:

Snapshot
    ↓
Restore
    ↓
New RDS Instance

Then:

  • test
  • verify
  • switch applications if needed

10.17 Why New Instance Restore is Important

Safer because:

  • original DB preserved
  • rollback possible
  • testing possible

10.18 Recovery Time

Restoration time depends on:

  • DB size
  • storage performance
  • region
  • workload

Large databases:

  • may take long time

10.19 Recovery Objectives

Two VERY important production concepts.

RTO (Recovery Time Objective)

Means:

How fast system recovers.

RPO (Recovery Point Objective)

Means:

How much data loss acceptable.

Example:

Lose at most 5 minutes of data

10.20 PITR Improves RPO

Because transaction logs captured continuously:

  • less data loss possible

10.21 Snapshot Storage

Snapshots stored separately from DB instance.

Meaning:

  • deleting DB does not necessarily remove snapshots

unless configured otherwise.

10.22 Final Snapshot Before Deletion

RDS can ask:

Create final snapshot before deletion?

Production answer usually:

YES

Very important safety feature.

10.23 Deletion Protection

RDS supports:

Deletion Protection

Prevents accidental deletion.

Very useful in production.

10.24 Backup Encryption

Backups can be encrypted using:

Amazon Web Services KMS.

Protects:

  • snapshots
  • automated backups
  • replicas

Important for:

  • compliance
  • enterprise systems

10.25 Cross-Region Snapshots

Snapshots can be copied across regions.

Example:

us-east-1
    ↓
eu-central-1

Useful for:

  • disaster recovery
  • region-level failures

10.26 Disaster Recovery (DR)

Disaster Recovery means:

Recovering from catastrophic failures.

Examples:

  • region outage
  • major corruption
  • ransomware
  • large-scale infrastructure failure

10.27 HA vs Backup

VERY important distinction.

FeatureHigh AvailabilityBackup/Recovery
PurposeMinimize downtimeRestore lost data
Handles crashesYesYes
Handles accidental deletionNoYes
Handles corruptionLimitedYes

Multi-AZ does NOT replace backups.

VERY important.

10.28 Example: Bad Deployment

Example:

DELETE FROM users;

replicates to:

  • Multi-AZ standby
  • replicas

So HA alone cannot save you.

You still need:

  • backups
  • PITR

10.29 Snapshot Use Cases

Common production uses:

  • before migrations
  • before upgrades
  • before risky deployments
  • cloning environments
  • testing

10.30 Cloning Database

Snapshots can create:

  • staging environments
  • test environments
  • analytics copies

Example:

Production Snapshot
      ↓
Create Staging DB

Very useful.

10.31 Logical Backups vs RDS Backups

RDS backups are:

  • infrastructure-level

Logical backups:

  • pg_dump
  • mysqldump

Differences:

TypePurpose
RDS SnapshotFull infrastructure restore
pg_dumpPortable logical export

Many companies use BOTH.

10.32 Why Companies Still Use pg_dump

Because:

  • portable
  • version migration easier
  • selective restore possible

RDS snapshots are AWS-specific.

10.33 Backup Monitoring

Important to monitor:

  • backup failures
  • retention
  • snapshot age
  • storage usage

Backup that cannot restore is useless.

10.34 Testing Recovery

VERY important production practice.

Companies should regularly:

  • test restore
  • verify backups
  • validate recovery process

Many companies discover broken backups too late.

10.35 Common Backup Mistakes

1. No Backups

Catastrophic risk.

2. Never Testing Recovery

Dangerous assumption.

3. Short Retention

Cannot recover older issues.

4. No Final Snapshot

Accidental deletion risk.

5. Relying Only on Multi-AZ

HA ≠ backup strategy.

10.36 Real Production Architecture

Typical setup:

Primary DB
    ↓
Automated Backups
    ↓
Snapshots
    ↓
Cross-region copy

Optional:

  • pg_dump exports
  • cold archive storage

10.37 Mental Model

Think like:

Current Database
      ↓
Snapshots
      ↓
Transaction Logs/WAL
      ↓
Recovery Capability

10.38 Real Production Insight

Most catastrophic outages are caused by:

  • human mistakes
  • bad deployments
  • accidental deletions

NOT hardware failures.

Backups protect against:

  • humans

which is extremely important.

10.39 Strong Interview Explanation

You can explain RDS backups and recovery like:

RDS provides automated backups and manual snapshots for recovery purposes. Automated backups combine storage snapshots with transaction logs or WAL logs to support Point-In-Time Recovery, allowing restoration to a specific timestamp within the retention window. Manual snapshots are persistent backups retained until manually deleted and are commonly used before migrations or major deployments. Backups improve durability and disaster recovery capabilities, while High Availability features like Multi-AZ focus primarily on minimizing downtime rather than recovering deleted or corrupted data.
Monitoring and Performance

11. Monitoring and Performance in RDS

Monitoring is how you understand:

  • database health
  • bottlenecks
  • overload
  • failures
  • scaling needs

Without monitoring:

Production debugging becomes blind guessing.

Monitoring is one of the BIGGEST differences between:

  • junior infrastructure
  • production-grade infrastructure

11.1 Why Monitoring Matters

Databases fail slowly before they fail completely.

Example symptoms:

  • slow queries
  • rising latency
  • CPU spikes
  • memory exhaustion
  • connection saturation
  • replication lag

Monitoring helps detect problems BEFORE outage.

11.2 High-Level Monitoring Architecture

RDS monitoring flow:

RDS Instance
      ↓
Metrics Collection
      ↓
CloudWatch / Performance Insights
      ↓
Dashboards + Alerts

11.3 Main Monitoring Systems in RDS

RDS integrates with:

ToolPurpose
CloudWatchInfrastructure metrics
Enhanced MonitoringOS-level metrics
Performance InsightsQuery-level analysis
RDS EventsDB event notifications

11.4 CloudWatch

Amazon Web Services CloudWatch is AWS monitoring service.

RDS automatically publishes metrics to CloudWatch.

Metrics include:

  • CPU
  • storage
  • connections
  • network throughput
  • replication lag

11.5 Main Metrics You MUST Know

Core RDS metrics:

- CPUUtilization
- FreeStorageSpace
- DatabaseConnections
- ReadIOPS
- WriteIOPS
- ReadLatency
- WriteLatency
- ReplicaLag
- FreeableMemory

VERY important interview topic.

11.6 CPU Utilization

Measures:

How busy DB CPU is.

High CPU may indicate:

  • heavy queries
  • missing indexes
  • too many connections
  • insufficient instance size

11.7 High CPU Example

Bad query:

SELECT * FROM huge_table;

without index may cause:

  • full table scan
  • CPU spike

11.8 Freeable Memory

Measures:

  • available RAM

Low memory causes:

  • disk swapping
  • slower queries
  • higher latency

11.9 Why RAM is Important

PostgreSQL heavily uses RAM for:

  • caching
  • sorting
  • indexes
  • query execution

Low memory:

  • storage reads increase
  • performance decreases

11.10 Database Connections

Measures:

  • active DB sessions

Too many connections can:

  • exhaust memory
  • overload DB
  • cause failures

11.11 Connection Saturation

Example error:

remaining connection slots are reserved

Usually caused by:

  • no connection pooling
  • leaked connections
  • traffic spikes

11.12 Read IOPS

Measures:

Read operations per second

High read IOPS:

  • heavy read workload

11.13 Write IOPS

Measures:

Write operations per second

High write IOPS:

  • transaction-heavy system
  • WAL pressure

11.14 Latency Metrics

Important metrics:

ReadLatency
WriteLatency

Meaning:

  • how long storage operations take

High latency:

  • slow queries
  • slow APIs

11.15 Storage Bottlenecks

Very important insight:

DB performance often limited by storage,
not CPU.

Especially:

  • analytics
  • large datasets
  • heavy writes

11.16 Free Storage Space

Measures:

  • remaining disk space

Low storage:

  • dangerous production risk

If storage fills:

  • writes may fail
  • DB may stop functioning

11.17 Replica Lag

For Read Replicas:

How far replica behind primary.

Large lag causes:

  • stale reads
  • inconsistent user experience

11.18 Enhanced Monitoring

Provides:

  • OS-level visibility

Shows:

  • CPU per process
  • memory usage
  • filesystem metrics
  • thread activity

More detailed than standard CloudWatch.

11.19 Performance Insights

One of the BEST RDS features.

Focuses on:

  • SQL query performance

Helps identify:

  • slow queries
  • bottlenecks
  • blocking queries
  • high-load SQL

VERY useful in production.

11.20 Why Query Monitoring Matters

Many DB problems are NOT infrastructure problems.

They are:

Bad SQL problems.

Example:

SELECT * FROM orders;

on huge table without indexes.

Monitoring helps find these.

11.21 Slow Queries

Slow queries cause:

  • high CPU
  • high latency
  • blocked connections
  • poor UX

Monitoring slow queries is critical.

11.22 Query Execution Time

Performance Insights can show:

  • which queries consume most time
  • which queries block others
  • query frequency

Very useful.

11.23 Query Plans

PostgreSQL can analyze query execution.

Example:

EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT * FROM users;

Shows:

  • index usage
  • scans
  • execution cost

VERY important optimization skill.

11.24 Full Table Scan

Dangerous pattern.

Example:

Sequential scan over millions of rows

Usually caused by:

  • missing indexes

11.25 Index Monitoring

Indexes improve:

  • read performance

But too many indexes:

  • slow writes
  • increase storage

Need balance.

11.26 Lock Monitoring

PostgreSQL uses locks for consistency.

Long transactions may:

  • block queries
  • freeze application behavior

Monitoring helps detect blocking.

11.27 Deadlocks

Deadlock:

Two transactions waiting on each other forever.

DB eventually kills one transaction.

Important production issue.

11.28 Transaction Monitoring

Long-running transactions:

  • consume resources
  • block VACUUM
  • increase WAL growth

Need monitoring.

11.29 WAL Monitoring

PostgreSQL generates:

  • WAL logs

Heavy write traffic:

  • increases WAL generation
  • affects replication
  • affects storage

Monitoring important.

11.30 Replication Monitoring

For replicas monitor:

  • lag
  • sync status
  • replica health

Lag spikes may indicate:

  • overloaded primary
  • network issues
  • slow replica

11.31 Alerts and Alarms

CloudWatch can trigger alarms.

Example:

CPU > 80%

or:

Free storage < 10 GB

Very important production practice.

11.32 Why Alerts Matter

Without alerts:

Problems discovered by users first.

Bad production practice.

Good systems:

  • alert engineers before outage

11.33 Logging

RDS logs include:

  • authentication failures
  • query errors
  • slow queries
  • startup/shutdown events

Useful for:

  • debugging
  • auditing
  • incident investigation

11.34 Common Performance Problems

1. Missing Indexes

Most common issue.

2. N+1 Queries

ORM issue.

Example:

1 query
   +
100 extra queries

Very inefficient.

3. Too Many Connections

Connection exhaustion.

4. Full Table Scans

Large CPU usage.

5. Storage Latency

Slow disk operations.

6. Large Transactions

Blocking + WAL pressure.

11.35 Query Optimization First

VERY important production principle:

Optimize queries before scaling hardware.

Many systems waste money scaling:

  • bad SQL

instead of fixing queries.

11.36 Scaling vs Optimization

Example:

Bad approach:

Huge expensive DB
running terrible queries

Better approach:

Optimized queries
with proper indexes

Often much cheaper and faster.

11.37 Real Production Monitoring Architecture

Typical setup:

RDS
  ↓
CloudWatch Metrics
  ↓
Dashboards + Alerts
  ↓
Engineers notified

Additional:

  • Performance Insights
  • Logs
  • Grafana
  • Prometheus integrations

11.38 Production Incident Example

Symptoms:

API latency spikes

Monitoring reveals:

  • CPU 95%
  • huge sequential scans
  • missing index

Solution:

  • add index
  • optimize query

Without monitoring:

  • impossible to diagnose quickly

11.39 Mental Model

Think of monitoring like:

Infrastructure Health
        +
Query Performance
        +
Storage Metrics
        +
Connection Metrics
        =
Database Visibility

11.40 Real Production Insight

Most database outages are NOT:

  • PostgreSQL bugs

Usually:

  • poor queries
  • overloaded connections
  • bad indexes
  • insufficient monitoring

Monitoring helps catch these early.

11.41 Strong Interview Explanation

You can explain RDS monitoring and performance like:

RDS monitoring is primarily handled through CloudWatch metrics, Enhanced Monitoring, and Performance Insights. CloudWatch provides infrastructure-level visibility such as CPU utilization, memory, storage, IOPS, latency, and connection counts, while Performance Insights focuses on SQL-level bottlenecks and slow queries. Effective monitoring allows teams to detect performance degradation, replication lag, storage exhaustion, and query inefficiencies before they cause production outages.
Amazon Aurora

12. Amazon Aurora

Amazon Aurora Aurora is AWS’s cloud-native relational database engine.

It is one of the MOST important advanced RDS topics.

Aurora was created because AWS realized:

Traditional relational databases
were not designed for cloud-native scaling.

So AWS built Aurora to:

  • improve scalability
  • improve replication
  • improve failover
  • improve storage architecture
  • reduce bottlenecks

12.1 What is Aurora?

Aurora is:

AWS-built relational database engine
compatible with PostgreSQL and MySQL

Important:

Aurora is NOT just normal PostgreSQL on RDS.

It is:

  • AWS-engineered database architecture
  • cloud-optimized relational system

12.2 Aurora Compatibility

Aurora supports:

CompatibilityMeaning
Aurora PostgreSQLPostgreSQL-compatible
Aurora MySQLMySQL-compatible

Applications usually require:

  • minimal changes

Example:

Prisma
Sequelize
Node.js
pg

can often work similarly.

12.3 Why AWS Built Aurora

Traditional RDS architecture has limitations.

Example traditional architecture:

DB Engine
    ↓
Single storage layer

Scaling and replication become difficult.

AWS wanted:

  • distributed storage
  • faster failover
  • faster replication
  • cloud-native architecture

12.4 High-Level Aurora Architecture

Aurora architecture:

Compute Layer
      ↓
Distributed Shared Storage Layer

VERY important difference.

12.5 Traditional RDS vs Aurora

Traditional RDS

DB Instance
    ↓
Attached Storage

Each instance has its own storage.

Aurora

Multiple Compute Nodes
        ↓
Shared Distributed Storage

Storage shared across cluster.

12.6 Aurora Cluster

Aurora uses:

Cluster Architecture

Instead of:

  • isolated standalone DB instance

Aurora cluster includes:

  • primary writer
  • replicas
  • shared storage

12.7 Aurora Storage Layer

One of Aurora’s biggest innovations.

Aurora storage:

  • distributed
  • replicated
  • self-healing

Across:

  • multiple AZs

12.8 Aurora Storage Replication

Aurora automatically replicates storage:

6 copies
across 3 AZs

VERY important feature.

This improves:

  • durability
  • availability
  • recovery speed

12.9 Why Aurora Failover is Faster

Traditional RDS failover:

New storage attachment

Aurora:

Shared storage already exists

Only compute role changes.

Result:

  • faster failover

12.10 Aurora Writer and Readers

Aurora architecture:

Writer Node
    ↓
Shared Storage
    ↓
Reader Nodes

Writer handles:

  • writes

Readers handle:

  • read scaling

12.11 Aurora Read Replicas

Aurora replicas are:

  • faster
  • lower lag
  • more integrated

than traditional RDS replicas.

Because replicas share:

  • distributed storage layer

12.12 Aurora Reader Endpoint

Aurora provides:

  • cluster endpoint
  • reader endpoint

Applications can use:

Reads → Reader Endpoint
Writes → Cluster/Writer Endpoint

Very useful architecture.

12.13 Aurora Performance

AWS claims Aurora can provide:

  • much higher throughput
  • lower latency

than standard PostgreSQL/MySQL RDS.

Because:

  • optimized storage engine
  • distributed architecture
  • reduced WAL overhead

12.14 Aurora Scaling

Aurora scales better because:

  • compute separated from storage
  • distributed storage layer

Can:

  • add readers easily
  • scale reads efficiently

12.15 Aurora Replication

Aurora replication is:

  • faster
  • lower latency

than standard asynchronous replica setup.

12.16 Aurora Failover

If writer fails:

Reader promoted to writer

Very quickly.

Aurora designed for:

  • fast recovery
  • minimal downtime

12.17 Aurora Storage Autoscaling

Aurora storage automatically grows.

You usually do NOT manually provision storage like normal RDS.

Very cloud-native behavior.

12.18 Aurora Serverless

Aurora supports:

Aurora Serverless

Meaning:

  • automatic compute scaling

Useful for:

  • unpredictable workloads
  • intermittent traffic

12.19 Aurora Serverless Flow

Traffic increases:

Aurora automatically increases compute

Traffic decreases:

Aurora scales down

Very interesting cloud concept.

12.20 Aurora Global Database

Aurora supports:

  • cross-region replication

Architecture:

Primary Region
      ↓
Secondary Regions

Useful for:

  • global applications
  • disaster recovery
  • low latency worldwide

12.21 Aurora vs Standard RDS

FeatureStandard RDSAurora
StorageAttached storageDistributed shared storage
ReplicationTraditionalCloud-native
Failover speedSlowerFaster
Read scalingGoodBetter
Storage autoscalingLimited/manualAutomatic
CostLowerHigher
ComplexitySimplerMore advanced

12.22 Aurora Cost

Aurora usually costs more than standard RDS.

Because:

  • advanced architecture
  • distributed storage
  • faster replication
  • additional infrastructure

Tradeoff:

Higher cost
=
Better scalability and HA

12.23 When Aurora Makes Sense

Good use cases:

  • high traffic systems
  • SaaS platforms
  • enterprise workloads
  • global applications
  • high availability systems

12.24 When Standard RDS is Enough

Many applications do NOT need Aurora.

Examples:

  • small systems
  • moderate traffic APIs
  • early-stage startups
  • student projects

Standard PostgreSQL RDS often enough.

12.25 Aurora and PostgreSQL Compatibility

Aurora PostgreSQL is:

  • PostgreSQL-compatible

But NOT identical to open-source PostgreSQL.

Some:

  • extensions
  • low-level features
  • behaviors

may differ.

Important production consideration.

12.26 Aurora and Connection Scaling

Aurora can handle:

  • many connections
  • distributed readers

But connection pooling still VERY important.

Aurora does NOT magically remove:

  • poor architecture
  • bad queries

12.27 Aurora and Query Optimization

Even Aurora still needs:

  • indexes
  • optimized SQL
  • efficient schema design

Many developers incorrectly assume:

Aurora solves bad SQL.

FALSE.

12.28 Aurora Storage Durability

Aurora designed for:

  • extremely high durability

Because storage replicated across:

  • multiple nodes
  • multiple AZs

12.29 Aurora Recovery

Aurora recovery often faster because:

  • distributed storage already available
  • replicas already synchronized

12.30 Aurora Reader Scaling

Architecture:

Application
   ├── Writes → Writer
   └── Reads  → Reader Endpoint

Very scalable.

12.31 Aurora vs Multi-AZ

Aurora already includes:

  • distributed HA architecture

Different from classic:

  • RDS Multi-AZ model

12.32 Aurora Mental Model

Think of Aurora like:

Cloud-native PostgreSQL/MySQL
with distributed AWS storage architecture

NOT just:

  • “faster PostgreSQL”

12.33 Common Misunderstandings

1. Aurora is NoSQL

FALSE.

Aurora is relational.

2. Aurora Removes Need for Optimization

FALSE.

Still requires:

  • indexes
  • pooling
  • query tuning

3. Aurora is Always Better

FALSE.

Depends on:

  • scale
  • traffic
  • cost
  • complexity

12.34 Real Production Architecture

Typical Aurora setup:

Users
   ↓
Backend Cluster
   ↓
Aurora Cluster
      ├── Writer
      └── Readers

12.35 Real Production Insight

Aurora shines MOST when:

  • traffic large
  • replicas important
  • failover speed critical
  • global scaling required

For many smaller apps:

  • standard RDS simpler and cheaper.

12.36 Strong Interview Explanation

You can explain Aurora like:

Amazon Aurora is an AWS-built cloud-native relational database engine compatible with PostgreSQL and MySQL. Unlike standard RDS architectures where each instance has attached storage, Aurora separates compute from a distributed shared storage layer replicated across multiple Availability Zones. This architecture enables faster failover, improved replication performance, automatic storage scaling, and more efficient read scaling using Aurora reader nodes and cluster endpoints.
RDS Production Architecture

13. RDS Production Architecture

This is where everything comes together.

Production architecture means:

How real systems are designed
to safely run databases at scale.

This section is EXTREMELY important because:

  • interviews ask these designs
  • real companies use these patterns
  • scalability depends on architecture
  • security depends on architecture

13.1 First Important Reality

Production systems are NOT:

Frontend
   ↓
Public Database

That is beginner architecture.

Real production systems use:

  • layered infrastructure
  • private networking
  • load balancing
  • connection pooling
  • HA
  • monitoring

13.2 Basic Production Architecture

Typical architecture:

Users
   ↓
CloudFront/CDN
   ↓
Load Balancer
   ↓
Backend Servers
   ↓
Private RDS PostgreSQL

Very common architecture.

13.3 Why Database Should Be Private

Production DBs should usually be:

Private

NOT publicly accessible.

Reason:

  • minimize attack surface
  • internal-only communication
  • stronger isolation

Architecture:

Internet
   ↓
Backend
   ↓
Private RDS

13.4 Typical AWS Components

Common stack:

LayerAWS Service
CDNCloudFront
Load BalancerALB
BackendEC2/ECS/EKS/Lambda
DatabaseRDS/Aurora
CacheRedis/ElastiCache
MonitoringCloudWatch

13.5 Backend Layer

Backend may run on:

  • EC2
  • ECS
  • Kubernetes
  • Lambda

Backend responsibilities:

  • authentication
  • business logic
  • validation
  • DB access
  • caching

13.6 Why Frontend NEVER Talks Directly to DB

Bad:

React Frontend
      ↓
RDS

Problems:

  • credentials exposed
  • security disaster
  • impossible access control
  • no validation layer

Correct:

Frontend
   ↓
Backend API
   ↓
RDS

13.7 Internal Networking

Production communication usually uses:

  • private IPs
  • VPC networking

Flow:

Backend EC2
      ↓ Private Network
Private RDS

Fast and secure.

13.8 Security Groups in Production

Typical SG rules:

Backend SG

Allow:
80/443 from Load Balancer

RDS SG

Allow:
5432 ONLY from Backend SG

VERY important.

13.9 Why SG-to-SG Rules Matter

Instead of:

Allow from IP addresses

Use:

Allow from Backend Security Group

Benefits:

  • dynamic infrastructure
  • autoscaling friendly
  • cleaner architecture

Very common production practice.

13.10 Connection Pooling in Production

Critical concept.

Without pooling:

Every request
creates new DB connection

Disaster under traffic.

Production systems use:

Connection Pools

Architecture:

Backend Requests
      ↓
Connection Pool
      ↓
Few reusable DB connections
      ↓
RDS

13.11 Why Pooling Matters

Benefits:

  • fewer DB connections
  • lower overhead
  • better scalability
  • lower latency

Very important for:

  • Node.js APIs
  • NestJS
  • Express
  • Prisma
  • Sequelize

13.12 Multi-AZ in Production

Most production RDS setups use:

Multi-AZ

Architecture:

Primary DB
      ↓
Synchronous Replication
      ↓
Standby DB

Purpose:

  • high availability
  • failover protection

13.13 Read Replicas in Production

Used for:

  • scaling reads
  • analytics
  • reports

Architecture:

Writes → Primary
Reads  → Replicas

Very common scaling strategy.

13.14 Read/Write Separation

Backend logic routes:

Critical writes
     ↓
Primary

Heavy reads
     ↓
Replicas

Important scalability concept.

13.15 Caching Layer

Production systems often add:

Redis cache.

Architecture:

Backend
   ↓
Redis Cache
   ↓
RDS

Purpose:

  • reduce DB load
  • faster responses

Very common.

13.16 Why Cache Matters

Without cache:

Every request hits DB

DB becomes bottleneck quickly.

Cache reduces:

  • repeated reads
  • latency
  • DB pressure

13.17 Monitoring Architecture

Production systems monitor:

  • CPU
  • memory
  • storage
  • query performance
  • replica lag
  • connections

Tools:

  • CloudWatch
  • Performance Insights
  • Grafana
  • Prometheus

13.18 Logging Architecture

Logs include:

  • slow queries
  • failed logins
  • errors
  • replication events

Important for:

  • debugging
  • auditing
  • incident investigation

13.19 Backup Architecture

Production systems use:

  • automated backups
  • snapshots
  • PITR
  • cross-region backups

Architecture:

RDS
   ↓
Snapshots
   ↓
Cross-region backup

13.20 Disaster Recovery Architecture

Advanced systems prepare for:

  • region outages
  • catastrophic failures

Possible architecture:

Primary Region
      ↓
Cross-region Replica
      ↓
Secondary Region

13.21 Bastion Host Architecture

Admins should NOT expose DB publicly.

Instead:

Laptop
   ↓
Bastion Host
   ↓
Private RDS

Much safer.

13.22 VPN Architecture

   ↓ VPN
Private VPC
   ↓
Private RDS

13.23 ECS/Kubernetes Architecture

Modern deployments may use:

  • ECS
  • EKS
  • Kubernetes

Architecture:

Containers
    ↓
Connection Pool
    ↓
Private RDS

13.24 Lambda and RDS

RDS Proxy manages:

   ↓

RDS

Aurora + Multi-AZ + Replicas

13.28 Small Startup Architecture

Typical early-stage:

   ↓
Single Backend
   ↓
Single RDS

Example:

Load Balancer
      ↓
Multiple Backend Servers

1. Public Database Exposure

Huge security risk.

2. No Connection Pooling

DB overload.

3. Missing Monitoring

4. No Read Scaling

13.32 Production Principles

Good production systems prioritize:

- security
- availability

13.33 Real Production Insight

Most production systems fail NOT because:

13.34 Mental Model

Think of production architecture like:

Users
   ↓
Edge/CDN
   ↓
Backend Layer
   ↓
Connection Layer
   ↓

13.35 Strong Interview Explanation

You can explain RDS production architecture like:

Production RDS architectures typically place databases in private subnets inside a VPC and expose them only to internal backend services such as EC2, ECS, Kubernetes, or Lambda workloads. High Availability is commonly implemented using Multi-AZ deployments, while Read Replicas and caching layers such as Redis improve scalability. Security Groups restrict database access to backend services only, and connection pooling is used to efficiently manage database sessions. Monitoring, backups, snapshots, and disaster recovery mechanisms are integrated to ensure reliability and operational visibility.

EC2
1. What Is EC2?

EC2 stands for:

Elastic Compute Cloud

It provides:

Virtual servers in the cloud

You can:

  • run applications
  • host websites
  • run databases
  • deploy APIs
  • run Docker containers
  • execute background jobs

Real Meaning

When you create EC2:

AWS gives you:

  • virtual RAM

inside AWS datacenters.

Important

EC2 is:

YOU manage:

  • Docker
  • Nginx
  • app deployment
  • security configs
2. Why “Elastic”?

Elastic means:

Scalable on demand

You can:

  • increase CPU/RAM
  • create more instances
  • terminate instances
  • auto-scale

within minutes.

3. Real Physical Architecture

You do NOT get real dedicated physical server (usually).

Instead:

Physical Server
    ↓
Hypervisor
    ↓
Multiple EC2 Virtual Machines

AWS virtualizes hardware.

Your EC2 is:

a virtual machine (VM)

Server template

Examples

  • Ubuntu

Real Analogy

AMI is like:

Operating system ISO/template

for creating servers.

Example

Ubuntu Linux VM

already preconfigured.

Instance type determines:

  • CPU

tfamily

7. Launching EC2 — What Actually Happens

When you click:

Launch Instance

AWS does:

Step 1 — Allocate Hardware

Selects physical host.

Step 2 — Create VM

Hypervisor creates isolated VM.

Step 3 — Attach Storage

Usually EBS volume attached.

Step 4 — Configure Networking

Assigns:

  • private IP
  • optional public IP
  • VPC networking

Step 5 — Boot Operating System

From AMI.

Step 6 — Apply Security Rules

Security groups attached.

Step 7 — Inject SSH Key

Your public key added.

Step 8 — Start VM

Linux boots.

8. EC2 Lifecycle

A. Pending

Launching.

B. Running

Active.

C. Stopped

VM shut down.

Can restart later.

EBS preserved.

D. Terminated

Destroyed permanently.

Cannot restart.

Important Difference

Stop

Like shutting down laptop.

Data on EBS survives.

Terminate

Like destroying machine permanently.

9. EBS (Elastic Block Store)

Most EC2 instances use:

Amazon EBS

What Is EBS?

Persistent block storage.

Like:

  • SSD/HDD attached to VM

Important

EC2 compute and storage are separate.

You can:

  • detach volume
  • attach elsewhere
  • snapshot backups
10. Instance Store vs EBS
Can we add instance storage to t3.micro

No, you cannot add an instance store to a t3.micro.
The t3 family belongs to a category of instances called EBS-only. They are physically hosted on hardware that does not have local disks available for virtual machines to use.

Hardware Limitation: t3.micro instances run on servers designed to use network storage (EBS) only. There is no physical "spare" drive on that host to give to you.Family Rules: Only specific instance families (mostly those with a "d" in the name, like m5d or c6gd) have the physical wiring to support instance stores.Launch Time Only: Even on supported instances, you must map the instance store at the moment of launch. You cannot "hot-plug" an instance store into a running machine later.

EBS

Persistent.

Survives stop/restart.

Instance Store

Temporary local disk.

Destroyed if instance stops.

Very fast.
