ECS Learning Table of Contents

1. Introduction to ECS

1.1 What is ECS

Definition

ECS stands for:

Elastic Container Service

It is a container orchestration service provided by Amazon Web Services.

ECS helps you:

  • run containers
  • manage containers
  • scale containers
  • monitor containers
  • deploy containers

without manually managing everything yourself.

Simple Analogy

Before ECS:

You manually start Docker containers on servers.

With ECS:

AWS automatically manages and orchestrates containers for you.

Real Problem ECS Solves

Imagine you have:

  • 10 Docker containers
  • 5 EC2 servers
  • production traffic
  • crashes
  • deployments
  • scaling

Without ECS:

You manually:

  • choose server
  • start containers
  • restart failed containers
  • distribute traffic
  • scale instances
  • monitor health

This becomes a nightmare.

ECS Automates This

ECS can:

  • start containers
  • restart crashed containers
  • distribute workloads
  • scale automatically
  • integrate with load balancers
  • deploy new versions

Very Important Understanding

ECS itself DOES NOT run applications directly.

ECS orchestrates Docker containers.

So internally:

Your App
   ↓
Docker Container
   ↓
ECS manages container

ECS Core Idea

ECS answers these questions automatically:

Where should container run?

ECS scheduler decides.

What if container crashes?

ECS restarts it.

What if traffic increases?

ECS scales tasks.

How to deploy new version?

ECS performs rolling deployments.

Real Production Example

Imagine your:

  • NestJS backend
  • PostgreSQL in Amazon Web Services RDS
  • React frontend in S3

Now instead of:

Running backend manually on EC2

you do:

Dockerize backend
   ↓
Push image to ECR
   ↓
ECS runs containers automatically

That is modern production infrastructure.

ECS Internally

ECS mainly consists of:

  • Cluster
  • Tasks
  • Services
  • Task Definitions

You will learn these deeply later.

For now think:

Cluster → group of machines

Task → running container

Service → keeps containers alive

Task Definition → blueprint/config

ECS vs EC2

This is VERY important.

EC2

You manage:

  • server
  • Docker
  • scaling
  • deployments
  • crashes
  • monitoring

ECS

AWS manages orchestration.

You focus mostly on:

  • application
  • Docker image
  • deployment config

ECS is NOT Docker

Many beginners confuse this.

Docker

Tool for creating/running containers.

ECS

Platform that MANAGES Docker containers at scale.

ECS Workflow Overview

Write Application
      ↓
Dockerize App
      ↓
Push Image to ECR
      ↓
Create ECS Task Definition
      ↓
Create ECS Service
      ↓
AWS Runs Containers

Why ECS Became Popular

Because companies needed:

  • microservices
  • scalable backend systems
  • auto deployments
  • fault tolerance
  • cloud-native infrastructure

Manual Docker management was not enough.

1.2 Why ECS exists

Before Containers

Old deployment:

Application directly installed on server

Problems:

  • dependency conflicts
  • difficult deployments
  • environment mismatch
  • scaling difficulties

Example:

Works on my machine
Fails on production

Classic problem.

Docker Solved Packaging

Docker introduced:

Package app + dependencies together

Now app runs consistently everywhere.

But another problem appeared.

New Problem After Docker

Imagine:

  • hundreds of containers
  • multiple servers
  • crashes
  • deployments
  • networking

Who manages all this?

Docker alone cannot solve orchestration at large scale.

ECS Solves Orchestration

ECS manages:

  • scheduling
  • scaling
  • deployment
  • recovery
  • networking
  • monitoring

ECS Exists Because of Scale

Running:

docker run app

for one container is easy.

Running:

300 containers across 50 servers

is hard.

That is why ECS exists.

1.3 Problems ECS solves

Problem 1 — Manual Container Management

Before ECS:

Imagine you have:

5 EC2 servers
20 Docker containers

You manually do:

docker run
dockerstop
dockerrestart

on different servers.

Real Problem

You must manually decide:

  • which server runs container
  • how many containers needed
  • what if server dies
  • what if container crashes
  • what if CPU becomes full

This becomes impossible at scale.

ECS Solution → Orchestration

ECS introduces:

Desired State Management

You tell ECS:

I want 4 containers running

ECS continuously ensures:

Running containers == Desired containers

This is one of the MOST IMPORTANT concepts in orchestration.

Internal Mechanism

ECS Service constantly checks:

Desired Count
vs
Actual Running Count

Example:

Desired = 4
Running = 3

ECS immediately creates new task.

This process is called:

Reconciliation Loop

Kubernetes works similarly.

Problem 2 — Container Crashes

Without ECS:

If Docker container crashes:

Application becomes unavailable

You manually restart:

dockerrestart

Bad for production.

ECS Solution → Self Healing

ECS continuously monitors task health.

If task dies:

Running = 3
Desired = 4

Scheduler automatically launches replacement.

Important Understanding

ECS Service behaves like:

Background supervisor process

continuously checking cluster state.

Problem 3 — Server Resource Allocation

Without ECS:

You manually choose:

Which EC2 should run which container?

Hard problems:

  • memory exhaustion
  • CPU exhaustion
  • uneven load
  • wasted resources

ECS Solution → Scheduler

ECS Scheduler checks:

  • available RAM
  • available CPU
  • placement rules
  • availability zone
  • networking

Then intelligently places containers.

Example

Suppose:

Task requires:
2 CPU
4GB RAM

ECS checks cluster machines:

Server A → insufficient RAM
Server B → enough resources

Task placed on:

Server B

Problem 4 — Traffic Spikes

Without ECS:

High traffic causes:

  • CPU overload
  • slow responses
  • crashes

Manual scaling too slow.

ECS Solution → Auto Scaling

ECS integrates with:

  • Amazon CloudWatch CloudWatch
  • Application Auto Scaling

Flow:

High CPU
   ↓
CloudWatch Alarm
   ↓
Scale ECS Tasks
   ↓
More Containers

Important Understanding

ECS scales:

containers/tasks

NOT requests directly.

More tasks:

More application instances

handle more traffic.

Problem 5 — Zero Downtime Deployments

Without ECS:

Deployment flow:

Stop old app
Deploy new app
Start new app

Problem:

Downtime

Users cannot access app.

ECS Solution → Rolling Deployments

ECS deploys gradually.

Example:

4 old containers

ECS process:

Start 1 new container
Check health
Stop 1 old container
Repeat

Users continue accessing app during deployment.

Internal Deployment Logic

ECS Service uses:

  • desired count
  • minimum healthy percent
  • maximum percent

to safely rotate containers.

Problem 6 — Load Distribution

Without ECS:

One container may receive:

90% traffic

while others idle.

ECS Solution → Load Balancer Integration

ECS integrates with:

  • Amazon Web Services ALB
  • Target Groups

Flow:

User Request
     ↓
ALB
     ↓
Healthy ECS Tasks

Traffic distributed automatically.

Problem 7 — Infrastructure Complexity

Without ECS:

You manually manage:

  • Docker
  • deployments
  • networking
  • scaling
  • health checks
  • recovery

Complex and error-prone.

ECS Solution → Abstraction Layer

ECS abstracts orchestration complexity.

You mostly define:

What should run

ECS handles:

How it should run

VERY important cloud-native principle.

Problem 8 — Multi-Container Applications

Modern systems:

API
Redis
Worker
Queue Processor

all communicate together.

Managing manually is difficult.

ECS Solution

ECS provides:

  • service discovery
  • networking
  • task grouping
  • communication management

Core ECS Philosophy

The MOST IMPORTANT concept in ECS:

Desired State Management

You declare:

"I want 4 healthy containers"

ECS continuously works to maintain that state.

This is the heart of orchestration systems.

1.5 ECS vs Kubernetes

1.5 ECS vs Kubernetes

This section is EXTREMELY important because many people incorrectly think:

ECS and Kubernetes are competitors

The REAL understanding is:

Both solve the SAME orchestration problem
but with different philosophies.

First Understand the Core Problem

Both:

  • ECS
  • Kubernetes

exist because managing containers manually becomes impossible at scale.

Both systems solve:

  • scheduling
  • scaling
  • self-healing
  • deployments
  • orchestration

High-Level Comparison

ECSKubernetes
AWS-nativeCloud agnostic
SimplerMore complex
Easier learning curveSteeper learning curve
Managed tightly by AWSUniversal ecosystem
Less flexibleExtremely flexible
Faster setupMore configuration
Smaller operational overheadLarger operational overhead

Core Philosophical Difference

ECS Philosophy

AWS manages orchestration for you

AWS tightly integrates everything.

You mainly configure:

  • tasks
  • services
  • scaling

Kubernetes Philosophy

Build universal orchestration platform

Kubernetes is designed to run:

  • anywhere
  • any cloud
  • any infrastructure

Much more flexible.

ECS Architecture

ECS Service
     ↓
ECS Scheduler
     ↓
Tasks/Containers

Simpler architecture.

AWS abstracts many internals.

Kubernetes Architecture

API Server
   ↓
Scheduler
   ↓
Controller Manager
   ↓
etcd
   ↓
Kubelet
   ↓
Pods

Much more complex distributed system.

Important Understanding

Kubernetes is basically:

A distributed operating system for containers

VERY sophisticated internally.

ECS is Simpler by Design

AWS intentionally made ECS:

  • opinionated
  • tightly integrated
  • easier to operate

This reduces operational complexity.

ECS Components

Main concepts:

  • Cluster
  • Task
  • Service
  • Task Definition

Very small learning surface.

Kubernetes Components

Huge ecosystem:

  • Pod
  • Deployment
  • ReplicaSet
  • StatefulSet
  • DaemonSet
  • Service
  • Ingress
  • ConfigMap
  • Secret
  • PersistentVolume
  • Namespace
  • CRD
  • Operator

Much larger complexity.

ECS vs Kubernetes Scheduling

ECS Scheduler

AWS-managed scheduler decides:

Where container should run

Mostly abstracted away.

Kubernetes Scheduler

Kubernetes scheduler extremely advanced.

Checks:

  • taints/tolerations
  • affinities
  • anti-affinities
  • topology spread
  • node selectors
  • resource quotas

Very configurable.

ECS Networking

ECS networking:

  • simpler
  • AWS-integrated
  • VPC-native

Especially with:

awsvpc mode

Kubernetes Networking

Kubernetes networking much more advanced and complex.

Requires:

  • CNI plugins
  • overlay networking
  • service mesh sometimes

Examples:

  • Calico
  • Flannel
  • Cilium

Deployment Complexity

ECS Deployment

Usually:

Docker image
   ↓
ECR
   ↓
ECS Service

Very straightforward.

Kubernetes Deployment

Usually:

Docker image
   ↓
Registry
   ↓
YAML manifests
   ↓
kubectl apply

Many moving parts.

ECS Operational Burden

Low operational burden.

AWS handles:

  • control plane
  • orchestration internals
  • integrations

Kubernetes Operational Burden

Higher operational burden.

Need understanding of:

  • cluster internals
  • control plane
  • networking
  • storage classes
  • ingress controllers
  • RBAC
  • etcd

Much deeper ecosystem.

ECS Learning Curve

Easier for:

  • startups
  • small teams
  • backend developers

You can become productive quickly.

Kubernetes Learning Curve

Steeper.

Requires:

  • DevOps knowledge
  • infrastructure understanding
  • distributed systems concepts

Flexibility Comparison

ECS

Opinionated:

AWS way of doing orchestration

Less customizable.

Kubernetes

Extremely extensible.

You can build:

  • custom schedulers
  • operators
  • CRDs
  • custom controllers

Much more powerful platform.

Kubernetes

Kubernetes Common In:

ECS

Lower operational complexity:

Less engineers needed

Kubernetes

Higher operational complexity:

More maintenance
More expertise

ECS vs Kubernetes Internally

ECS

More:

Managed orchestration service

Kubernetes

More:

Container orchestration platform ecosystem

Much broader scope.

ECS and EKS

VERY important distinction.

which is:

ServiceMeaning

Based on your path:

could run as:

Example

Suppose:

User uploads image

2. Docker Fundamentals for ECS (Review)

This section is IMPORTANT because internally ECS is basically:

Container orchestration over Docker containers

If Docker concepts are weak:

ECS internals will not fully make sense

2.1 What are Containers

Container = isolated runtime environment for application.

Contains:

  • application code
  • dependencies
  • runtime
  • libraries
  • environment config

Key Idea

Instead of:

Installing app directly on OS

you package:

Everything app needs

inside container.

Container Characteristics

FeatureMeaning
IsolationSeparate runtime
PortabilityRuns everywhere
LightweightShares host kernel
Fast startupFaster than VMs
ReproducibleSame environment

VM vs Container

Virtual Machine

Hardware
  ↓
Hypervisor
  ↓
Guest OS
  ↓
Application

Heavy.

Container

Host OS Kernel
    ↓
Container Runtime
    ↓
Containers

Lightweight.

Important Internal Understanding

Containers DO NOT have separate kernels.

Containers share:

Host Linux kernel

Isolation provided using:

  • namespaces
  • cgroups

VERY important senior-level understanding.

Docker Uses

Linux kernel features:

  • PID namespace
  • network namespace
  • mount namespace
  • cgroups

to create isolation.

2.2 Docker Architecture

High-Level Architecture

Docker Client
      ↓
Docker Daemon
      ↓
Containers / Images / Networks / Volumes

Docker Client

CLI:

docker build
docker run
docker ps

sends API requests.

Docker Daemon

Main background process:

dockerd

Responsible for:

  • building images
  • creating containers
  • networking
  • storage management

Important Internal Flow

docker run nginx

actually means:

CLI
 ↓
Docker API request
 ↓
Docker daemon
 ↓
Create container

Container Runtime

Docker internally uses:

containerd

which eventually uses:

runc

to create actual containers.

VERY important modern Docker understanding.

Modern Docker Stack

Docker CLI
    ↓
Docker Daemon
    ↓
containerd
    ↓
runc
    ↓
Linux Kernel Features

2.3 Docker Images

Image = immutable blueprint/template.

Contains:

  • filesystem
  • dependencies
  • runtime
  • app code

Important Understanding

Image is:

READ-ONLY TEMPLATE

Container is:

RUNNING INSTANCE OF IMAGE

Exactly like:

Class → Object

Image Layers

Docker images built in layers.

Example:

FROM node:22
COPY package.json .
RUN npm install
COPY . .

Each instruction creates layer.

Why Layers Matter

Benefits:

  • caching
  • faster builds
  • layer reuse
  • efficient storage

Union File System

Docker combines layers using:

Union filesystem

Important for performance.

Image Lifecycle

Dockerfile
   ↓
docker build
   ↓
Docker Image
   ↓
docker push
   ↓
Registry

2.4 Docker Containers

Container = running process from image.

Internally Container Is Just:

Isolated Linux process

VERY important.

NOT virtual machine.

Container Lifecycle

Created
  ↓
Running
  ↓
Stopped
  ↓
Removed

Container Writable Layer

Images immutable.

Containers add:

temporary writable layer

Changes disappear after container removal unless volumes used.

Container Isolation

Containers isolated by:

  • filesystem namespaces
  • process namespaces
  • networking namespaces

Important ECS Connection

ECS tasks internally run:

Docker containers

Everything here directly maps into ECS.

Dockerfile = build instructions for image.

Example

COPY . .

EXPOSE 3000

Important Instructions

InstructionPurpose
FROMBase image
WORKDIRWorking directory
COPYCopy files
RUNExecute during build
ENVEnvironment variable
EXPOSEMetadata port
CMDDefault startup command

Build Process

docker build -t app .

Docker:

  • parses Dockerfile
  • executes layers
  • creates image

Dockerfile Optimization

Important:

  • layer caching
  • minimizing image size
  • multi-stage builds

Multi-Stage Builds

Very important production optimization.

Example:

Builder stage
 ↓
Compile app
 ↓
Copy only final artifacts

Smaller production images.

Docker provides virtual networking.

Network Types

NetworkPurpose

172.x.x.x

Port Mapping

means:

Host Port → Container Port

ECS networking heavily builds upon:

  • container networking
  • ENIs

  • namespaces

Container DNS

Docker provides internal DNS resolution.

Containers can communicate by:

container names

outside container lifecycle.

tmpfsIn-memory storage

  • EFS volumes

before starting containers.

3. ECS Core Architecture

3.1 ECS clusters

3.1 ECS Clusters

What is an ECS Cluster

An ECS Cluster is:

A logical grouping of infrastructure where your containers run.

Think of it like:

Container Environment

or:

A pool of compute resources

Inside the cluster, ECS places and manages your containers.

Real Mental Model

Imagine:

AWS Account
 └── ECS
      └── Production Cluster
            ├── Backend Containers
            ├── Auth Containers
            ├── Redis Containers
            └── Worker Containers

Cluster itself does NOT run containers.

Instead:

  • It organizes infrastructure
  • ECS schedules tasks inside it
  • Services live inside it
  • Tasks run inside it

Why Clusters Exist

Without clusters:

  • Everything mixes together
  • No separation between environments
  • Hard to manage permissions
  • Hard to scale
  • Hard to isolate workloads

Clusters provide:

BenefitExplanation
IsolationSeparate dev/staging/prod
OrganizationGroup related services
ScalingScale independently
SecurityDifferent IAM/network configs
MonitoringEasier metrics/logs
Resource managementControl compute usage

Types of ECS Clusters

ECS supports two infrastructure models.

1. EC2-backed Cluster

In this model:

YOU manage servers.

Architecture:

ECS Cluster
 └── EC2 Instances
      ├── Docker
      ├── ECS Agent
      └── Running Containers

You are responsible for:

  • EC2 sizing
  • OS updates
  • Scaling servers
  • Patching
  • Capacity planning

Flow

You create EC2
→ Install ECS Agent
→ Join cluster
→ ECS deploys containers there

Example

Cluster:
production-cluster

EC2 Instances:
- t3.medium
- t3.large
- m5.large

ECS schedules tasks across these machines.

Advantages of EC2 Cluster

AdvantageExplanation
Full controlYou manage servers
GPU supportML/AI workloads
Custom AMIsSpecial OS/software
Cheaper at scaleBetter long-term cost
Advanced networkingDeep customization

Disadvantages

ProblemExplanation
Server managementYou maintain infrastructure
Scaling complexityNeed ASG tuning
PatchingYour responsibility
Capacity planningMust predict usage

2. Fargate-backed Cluster

This is serverless containers.

You DO NOT manage servers.

Architecture:

ECS Cluster
 └── AWS-managed infrastructure
       └── Containers

You only define:

  • CPU
  • Memory
  • Container image
  • Networking

AWS handles:

  • Servers
  • Scaling
  • Patching
  • Infrastructure
  • Capacity

Flow

You create task
→ ECS launches Fargate runtime
→ Container starts automatically

No EC2 visible.

Advantages of Fargate

AdvantageExplanation
No server managementHuge simplicity
Easy scalingAWS handles infra
Better isolationEach task isolated
Faster setupMinimal ops
Secure by defaultStrong isolation

Disadvantages

ProblemExplanation
More expensiveUsually higher cost
Less controlNo host access
No custom kernelLimited low-level access
Limited GPU supportCompared to EC2

Which One is Used More?

Modern companies often prefer:

ECS + Fargate

because:

  • Easier
  • Faster
  • Less DevOps burden
  • Good for microservices

Large-scale/high-performance systems may use:

ECS + EC2

for cost optimization.

Cluster Capacity

Cluster capacity means:

How much compute exists

For EC2:

Capacity = EC2 resources

Example:

4 EC2 instances
Each:
- 4 vCPU
- 8 GB RAM

Total:
- 16 vCPU
- 32 GB RAM

ECS schedules tasks according to available resources.

In Fargate

Capacity is abstracted.

AWS dynamically allocates resources.

You only request:

CPU: 1 vCPU
RAM: 2GB

AWS finds infrastructure automatically.

ECS Cluster Internals

Inside ECS cluster:

Cluster
 ├── Services
 ├── Tasks
 ├── Capacity Providers
 ├── Container Instances
 └── Networking

Container Instance

IMPORTANT:

Container instance means:

EC2 instance registered into ECS cluster

NOT Docker container.

This confuses many beginners.

ECS Agent

EC2-based clusters use ECS Agent.

It is software running on EC2 instance.

Responsibilities:

  • Talks to ECS control plane
  • Receives tasks
  • Starts/stops containers
  • Reports health
  • Reports metrics

Architecture:

AWS ECS Control Plane
        ↑
   ECS Agent
        ↑
Docker Engine

Cluster Networking

Tasks inside cluster communicate through:

  • VPC
  • Subnets
  • Security Groups
  • ENIs
  • Service Discovery

This becomes VERY important later.

Cluster Auto Scaling

ECS can scale infrastructure automatically.

Example:

Traffic increases
→ More tasks needed
→ More EC2 instances launched

This is done using:

  • Auto Scaling Groups
  • Capacity Providers

Capacity Providers

Capacity provider decides:

Where tasks should run

Example:

70% Fargate
30% Fargate Spot

or:

Specific EC2 Auto Scaling Group

Real Production Example

Example architecture:

Production Cluster
 ├── API Service
 │    ├── 4 Tasks
 │    └── Load Balancer
 │
 ├── Worker Service
 │    ├── 10 Tasks
 │    └── Queue Consumer
 │
 ├── Notification Service
 │    └── 2 Tasks
 │
 └── Redis

All live inside same cluster.

ECS Cluster vs Kubernetes Cluster

Very important.

Both are:

Container orchestration clusters

Difference:

ECSKubernetes
AWS managedMore generic
EasierMore complex
AWS-nativeCloud agnostic
Simpler setupMore flexible
Less operational burdenMore control

Common Beginner Mistake

Many think:

Cluster = Server

Wrong.

Cluster is:

Logical orchestration boundary

Actual compute comes from:

  • EC2
  • Fargate

Production Best Practices

Separate Environments

Use different clusters:

dev-cluster
staging-cluster
prod-cluster

Never mix production and development.

Use Tags

Tag clusters:

Environment=Production
Team=Backend
Project=CRM

Monitor Clusters

Use:

  • CloudWatch
  • ECS metrics
  • Container Insights

Prefer Fargate Initially

Unless you truly need EC2 control.

Important Interview Question

Question

What is the difference between ECS Cluster and ECS Service?

Answer

Cluster:

Infrastructure boundary

Service:

Keeps tasks running

Cluster contains services.

Service manages tasks.

Real-Life Analogy

Imagine:

Cluster = City
Service = Restaurant chain
Task = Restaurant branch
Container = Workers inside branch

Deep Architecture View

Internet
   ↓
ALB
   ↓
ECS Service
   ↓
Tasks
   ↓
Containers
   ↓
Cluster
   ↓
EC2/Fargate Infrastructure

3.2 ECS tasks

3.2 ECS Tasks

What is an ECS Task

An ECS Task is:

A running instance of a Task Definition.

This is VERY important.

Simple Mental Model

Task Definition = Blueprint
Task = Running application

Like:

Class → Object
Docker Image → Running Container
Task Definition → Task

Real Example

Suppose you define:

Backend Application
- Node.js container
- 512 CPU
- 1GB RAM
- Port 4000

This is ONLY a definition.

When ECS actually launches it:

Running backend container

THAT becomes a task.

Architecture

Task Definition
      ↓
 ECS launches
      ↓
Task
      ↓
Containers running

Important Thing

A task can contain:

  • One container

    OR

  • Multiple containers

This is extremely important in microservices.

Single Container Task

Example:

Task
 └── Backend Container

Simple API service.

Multi-container Task

Example:

Task
 ├── Backend Container
 ├── Nginx Container
 └── Logging Sidecar

All run together.

All share:

  • Lifecycle
  • Networking
  • Storage (sometimes)

Why Multiple Containers in One Task?

Because some containers are tightly coupled.

Example:

Main App + Monitoring Agent

or:

App + Log Collector

Sidecar Pattern

Very important architecture concept.

Example:

Task
 ├── App Container
 └── FluentBit Container

FluentBit collects logs from app container.

This is called:

Sidecar container

Common in production systems.

ECS Task Lifecycle

Task goes through states.

1. PROVISIONING

ECS prepares infrastructure.

Example:

  • Allocating ENI
  • Preparing resources

2. PENDING

Task waiting to start.

Example:

  • Pulling Docker image
  • Preparing container runtime

3. RUNNING

Containers are active.

Application works.

4. STOPPED

Task terminated.

Reasons:

  • Manual stop
  • Crash
  • Deployment replacement
  • Health check failure

Lifecycle Flow

PROVISIONING
      ↓
PENDING
      ↓
RUNNING
      ↓
STOPPED

Task vs Container

This confuses MANY beginners.

Container

Actual Docker process.

Example:

node app.js

Task

Wrapper around one or more containers.

Example:

Task
 ├── Node Container
 └── Redis Sidecar

Important Difference

TaskContainer
ECS conceptDocker concept
Can contain many containersSingle process runtime
Managed by ECSManaged by Docker/containerd

Task Networking

Each task gets networking configuration.

In Fargate:

Usually:

1 Task = 1 ENI = 1 private IP

VERY important.

This gives strong isolation.

Example

Task A → 10.0.1.15
Task B → 10.0.1.16

Each behaves almost like its own mini-server.

Task Resources

Every task defines:

  • CPU
  • Memory

Example:

CPU: 512
Memory: 1024

ECS CPU Units

ECS uses CPU units.

Conversion:

CPU UnitsMeaning
2560.25 vCPU
5120.5 vCPU
10241 vCPU
20482 vCPU

Example

Task:
- 512 CPU
- 1024 Memory

Means:

0.5 vCPU
1GB RAM

Fargate Restrictions

Fargate allows only specific CPU-memory combinations.

Example:

CPUAllowed Memory
256512MB–2GB
5121GB–4GB
10242GB–8GB

Because AWS allocates predefined infrastructure.

Task Placement

ECS Scheduler decides:

Where task should run

In EC2 Mode

Scheduler checks:

  • Available CPU
  • Available memory
  • Placement constraints
  • Availability zones

Then selects EC2 instance.

In Fargate

AWS handles placement automatically.

You don't see servers.

Task Placement Strategies

ECS supports placement strategies.

Binpack

Pack tasks tightly.

Example:

Use minimum EC2 instances possible

Cost optimization.

Spread

Distribute tasks evenly.

Example:

Across AZs
Across EC2 instances

High availability.

Random

Random placement.

Rarely used.

Task Health Checks

Tasks can become unhealthy.

ECS monitors:

  • Container health checks
  • Load balancer health checks

Example

GET /health

If failing:

ECS kills task
→ launches replacement

Self-healing system.

Essential Containers

Inside task definition:

essential: true

Means:

If this container dies,
entire task dies.

Example

App container → essential
Monitoring container → non-essential

If monitoring crashes:

Task still runs

If app crashes:

Task stops

Task Storage

Tasks may use storage.

Ephemeral Storage

Temporary.

Destroyed when task stops.

Persistent Storage

Using:

  • EFS
  • EBS (EC2 mode)

For durable data.

Task IAM Role

VERY IMPORTANT.

Tasks can have IAM permissions.

Example:

Task can:
- Read S3
- Access SQS
- Write CloudWatch logs

Without hardcoding credentials.

Example

Backend Task
 └── IAM Role
       ├── s3:GetObject
       └── sqs:SendMessage

This is HUGE Security Best Practice

Never do:

AWS_ACCESS_KEY=...

Instead:

Use Task Role

Task Execution Role vs Task Role

Very important interview topic.

Task Execution Role

Used by ECS itself.

Example:

  • Pull image from ECR
  • Send logs to CloudWatch

Task Role

Used by your application.

Example:

  • Access S3
  • Access DynamoDB

Example Architecture

Task
 ├── Execution Role
 │      └── Pull image
 │
 └── Task Role
        └── App accesses S3

Standalone Task

Tasks can run independently.

Example:

Run database migration
Run cron job
Run one-time script

Without service.

Service-managed Tasks

Most production tasks are managed by ECS Service.

Example:

Desired count = 3

ECS always keeps 3 tasks alive.

Real Production Example

ECS Service
 ├── Task 1
 ├── Task 2
 └── Task 3

Each task may contain:

Nginx + Node.js

Task Scaling

ECS can scale tasks automatically.

Example:

CPU > 70%
→ Launch more tasks

This is:

Horizontal scaling

Rolling Deployment

When deploying new version:

Old tasks stopped gradually
New tasks started gradually

Without downtime.

ECS Task vs Kubernetes Pod

VERY IMPORTANT.

Closest Kubernetes equivalent:

ECSKubernetes
TaskPod
Task DefinitionPod Spec

Both:

  • Group containers
  • Share lifecycle
  • Share networking

Common Beginner Mistakes

Mistake 1

Thinking task definition is running.

Wrong.

Definition is blueprint only.

Mistake 2

Thinking one task = one container always.

Wrong.

Tasks may contain multiple containers.

Mistake 3

Confusing service with task.

Service manages tasks.

Task runs containers.

Real Architecture Flow

Task Definition
      ↓
Service
      ↓
Tasks
      ↓
Containers
      ↓
Application

Production Best Practices

Keep Tasks Stateless

Do not store data inside container filesystem.

Use:

  • S3
  • RDS
  • Redis
  • EFS

Use Health Checks

Always expose:

/health

Use Task Roles

Never hardcode AWS credentials.

Keep One Main Responsibility

Avoid huge multi-container tasks unless tightly coupled.

Interview Question

Question

What happens if ECS task crashes?

Answer

If managed by ECS Service:

ECS detects failure
→ launches replacement task

Self-healing architecture.

Deep Mental Model

Task Definition
   = Blueprint

Task
   = Running workload

Container
   = Actual process

3.3 ECS services

3.3 ECS Services

What is an ECS Service

An ECS Service is:

A long-running manager that keeps ECS tasks running continuously.

This is one of the MOST important ECS concepts.

Simple Mental Model

Task = Single running instance
Service = Task manager

Real Example

Suppose you want:

Always keep 3 backend containers running

Without service:

  • If container crashes → dead
  • If EC2 dies → dead
  • No automatic recovery

With ECS Service:

ECS continuously monitors tasks
and recreates them if needed

Core Responsibility of ECS Service

ECS Service ensures:

Desired number of tasks are always running

Example

Desired Count = 3

If one task crashes:

Running Tasks = 2

ECS immediately launches another:

Running Tasks = 3

This is called:

Self-healing

Architecture

Service
 ├── Task 1
 ├── Task 2
 └── Task 3

Service controls tasks.

Service Lifecycle

Step 1 — Create Task Definition

Blueprint.

Example:

Node.js API
Port 4000
512 CPU
1GB RAM

Step 2 — Create Service

Example:

Desired Count = 3

Step 3 — ECS Launches Tasks

Service
 ├── Task A
 ├── Task B
 └── Task C

Step 4 — ECS Monitors Tasks

If task dies:

Replace automatically

Why Services Exist

Without services:

  • No self-healing
  • No scaling
  • No deployments
  • No traffic balancing
  • No high availability

Service solves all of these.

Desired Count

VERY important.

Desired count means:

How many task instances should exist

Example

Desired Count = 5

ECS tries to maintain:

Exactly 5 tasks

at all times.

Service Scheduler

ECS Service contains scheduler logic.

Scheduler decides:

Where tasks should run

depending on:

  • CPU
  • Memory
  • AZ distribution
  • Placement strategy
  • Capacity providers

ECS Service vs Task

VERY important distinction.

ServiceTask
ManagerRunning workload
Maintains desired stateExecutes application
Long-livedCan stop anytime
Controls scalingRuns containers

Example

Service:
backend-service

Tasks:
backend-task-1
backend-task-2
backend-task-3

ECS Service + Load Balancer

This is how production systems usually work.

Architecture:

Internet
   ↓
ALB
   ↓
ECS Service
   ↓
Tasks

Why Load Balancer is Needed

Tasks may:

  • Crash
  • Restart
  • Scale dynamically
  • Get new IP addresses

Load balancer provides:

Stable entry point

Dynamic Task IP Problem

Example:

Task A → 10.0.1.5
Task B → 10.0.1.9
Task C → 10.0.2.4

These may change constantly.

Users cannot directly target tasks.

ALB solves this.

Service Discovery

ECS Services can register into service discovery.

Example:

auth-service.local
payment-service.local

Microservices communicate internally.

High Availability

Services distribute tasks across:

  • Multiple Availability Zones
  • Multiple EC2 instances

Example:

AZ-1 → 2 tasks
AZ-2 → 2 tasks

If one AZ dies:

Service still works

ECS Deployments

One of the BIGGEST jobs of service.

Service manages deployments.

Rolling Deployment

Example:

Current version:

v1

Deploy new version:

v2

ECS gradually replaces tasks.

Flow

Old Task
↓
New Task starts
↓
Health check passes
↓
Old Task removed

No downtime.

Deployment Configuration

Two VERY important settings.

Minimum Healthy Percent

Controls:

How many old tasks must stay alive

Maximum Percent

Controls:

How many extra tasks may temporarily exist

Example

Suppose:

Desired Count = 4
Minimum Healthy = 50%
Maximum Percent = 200%

During deployment:

  • Minimum running tasks = 2
  • Maximum temporary tasks = 8

Service Auto Scaling

Services can scale tasks automatically.

Example:

CPU > 70%
→ increase tasks

or:

Requests > threshold
→ scale out

Horizontal Scaling

Scaling services means:

Adding more tasks

NOT increasing CPU of single container.

Example

2 Tasks
→
10 Tasks

ECS Service Types

Replica Service

Most common.

Example:

Desired Count = 5

Keep 5 tasks alive.

Daemon Service

One task per EC2 instance.

Example:

Monitoring agent
Logging agent
Security scanner

Architecture:

EC2-1 → 1 monitoring task
EC2-2 → 1 monitoring task
EC2-3 → 1 monitoring task

Very similar to Kubernetes DaemonSet.

Service Placement

ECS decides where to place tasks.

Spread Strategy

Distribute tasks evenly.

Example:

Across Availability Zones

Better availability.

Binpack Strategy

Pack tasks tightly.

Example:

Use fewer EC2 instances

Better cost optimization.

Service Health Checks

Health checks are CRITICAL.

Container Health Check

Inside container:

GET /health

Load Balancer Health Check

ALB checks:

Is task responding?

If Task Fails

Service removes unhealthy task
→ launches replacement

ECS Service Networking

Tasks in service usually get:

  • Private IP
  • ENI
  • Security Groups

ALB forwards traffic internally.

Example Architecture

Internet
   ↓
Public ALB
   ↓
Private ECS Tasks

Very common production pattern.

ECS Service Events

Service emits events like:

Task failed health checks
Task started
Task stopped
Deployment completed

Useful for debugging.

Service Stability

Service tries to maintain:

Desired state

This is core orchestration concept.

Desired State vs Actual State

Example:

Desired:
3 Tasks

Actual:
2 Tasks

ECS reconciles difference.

This concept exists in:

  • ECS
  • Kubernetes
  • Docker Swarm

VERY important distributed systems principle.

ECS Service vs Kubernetes Deployment

Closest Kubernetes equivalent:

ECSKubernetes
ServiceDeployment
TaskPod

Common Beginner Mistakes

Mistake 1

Thinking tasks survive forever.

Wrong.

Tasks are ephemeral.

Services recreate them.

Mistake 2

Confusing ECS Service with networking service.

ECS Service is orchestration manager.

NOT network service.

Mistake 3

Using standalone tasks for production APIs.

Wrong.

Production APIs should use services.

Real Production Example

backend-service
 ├── 4 API tasks
 ├── Auto Scaling
 ├── ALB integration
 ├── Health checks
 └── Rolling deployments

Service Deployment Strategies

ECS supports:

  • Rolling update
  • Blue/Green deployment

Blue/Green

Advanced deployment pattern.

Architecture:

Blue = old version
Green = new version

Traffic gradually switches.

Usually implemented with:

AWS CodeDeploy

ECS Service Deep Internal Flow

Desired Count
      ↓
Scheduler
      ↓
Task Placement
      ↓
Task Launch
      ↓
Health Checks
      ↓
Continuous Monitoring

Interview Question

Question

What happens if an ECS task becomes unhealthy?

Answer

If task belongs to ECS Service:

ECS stops unhealthy task
→ launches replacement task
→ maintains desired count

Real Mental Model

Task
   = Worker

Service
   = Manager supervising workers

Production Best Practices

Always Use Services for APIs

Avoid standalone tasks for long-running apps.

Configure Health Checks

Mandatory for production.

Use Multiple AZs

High availability.

Use Auto Scaling

Prevent overload.

Use ALB

Never expose task IPs directly.

Full Architecture View

Users
   ↓
ALB
   ↓
ECS Service
   ↓
Tasks
   ↓
Containers
   ↓
Application

3.4 Task definitions

3.4 ECS Task Definitions

What is a Task Definition

A Task Definition is:

A blueprint that describes how ECS should run your containers.

VERY important:

Task Definition itself does NOT run anything.

It is ONLY configuration.

Mental Model

Task Definition = Blueprint
Task = Running instance

Exactly like:

Class → Object
Docker Image → Container
Task Definition → Task

What Does Task Definition Contain?

It defines:

  • Container image
  • CPU
  • Memory
  • Ports
  • Environment variables
  • Logging
  • IAM roles
  • Volumes
  • Networking
  • Health checks
  • Startup commands

Basically:

How containers should run

Real Example

Example backend API task definition:

Backend API
- Image: node-api:latest
- CPU: 512
- Memory: 1024
- Port: 4000
- ENV: DATABASE_URL

This is ONLY blueprint.

When ECS launches it:

Running task appears

Architecture Flow

Task Definition
      ↓
ECS Service / RunTask
      ↓
Task
      ↓
Containers

Task Definition Revisions

VERY IMPORTANT.

Task definitions are immutable.

Meaning:

You do NOT edit existing version.

Instead:

You create NEW revision.

Example

backend-api:1
backend-api:2
backend-api:3

Each revision is separate.

Why Revisions Exist

Because deployments must be reproducible.

Example:

Version 5 worked
Version 6 broken

Rollback becomes easy.

ECS Deployment Flow

Create new task definition revision
        ↓
Update ECS Service
        ↓
New tasks launched
        ↓
Old tasks removed

Main Sections of Task Definition

1. Family

Logical name.

Example:

"family": "backend-api"

2. Container Definitions

MOST important section.

Defines containers.

Example:

"containerDefinitions": []

3. CPU & Memory

Defines compute resources.

Example:

"cpu": "512",
"memory": "1024"

4. Network Mode

Defines networking model.

Example:

"networkMode": "awsvpc"

5. IAM Roles

Defines permissions.

Example:

"taskRoleArn": "...",
"executionRoleArn": "..."

6. Volumes

Persistent/shared storage.

Example:

"volumes": []

Simplified Full Example

{
  "family": "backend-api",
  "cpu": "512",
  "memory": "1024",
  "networkMode": "awsvpc",

  "containerDefinitions": [
    {
      "name": "api",
      "image": "my-api:latest",
      "essential": true,
      "portMappings": [
        {
          "containerPort": 4000
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

Container Definitions Deep Dive

This is heart of task definition.

Container Name

"name": "api"

Logical container name.

Image

Docker image to run.

"image": "123456789.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/api:latest"

Usually stored in:

Amazon Elastic Container Registry

which we will learn later.

Essential Flag

VERY important.

"essential": true

Means:

If container dies,
task dies.

Example

App Container → essential
Log Agent → non-essential

Port Mappings

Defines exposed ports.

Example:

"portMappings": [
  {
    "containerPort": 4000,
    "hostPort": 4000
  }
]

Container Port vs Host Port

VERY important.

Container Port

Port INSIDE container.

Example:

Node app listens on 4000

Host Port

Port on EC2 host machine.

Example

Host:4000 → Container:4000

Traffic forwarding.

In Fargate

Usually:

hostPort = containerPort

because tasks get dedicated ENI.

Environment Variables

Very common.

Example:

"environment": [
  {
    "name": "NODE_ENV",
    "value": "production"
  }
]

Sensitive Secrets

NEVER hardcode secrets directly.

Bad:

"DB_PASSWORD": "123456"

Use:

  • AWS Secrets Manager
  • SSM Parameter Store

Example

"secrets": [
  {
    "name": "DB_PASSWORD",
    "valueFrom": "arn:aws:ssm:..."
  }
]

Logging Configuration

Very important in production.

Example:

"logConfiguration": {
  "logDriver": "awslogs"
}

Logs sent to:

Amazon CloudWatch

Health Checks

Task definition can define health checks.

Example:

"healthCheck": {
  "command": [
    "CMD-SHELL",
    "curl -f http://localhost:4000/health || exit 1"
  ]
}

Why Health Checks Matter

If app hangs:

ECS detects unhealthy container
→ replaces task

Self-healing.

Entry Point & Command

Override Docker startup behavior.

Example:

"command": ["npm", "run", "start"]

Equivalent:

docker run image npm run start

Working Directory

Example:

"workingDirectory": "/app"

Resource Limits

Task definitions define limits.

CPU

"cpu": 512

Memory Hard Limit

Container killed if exceeded.

"memory": 1024

Memory Soft Limit

Preferred memory reservation.

"memoryReservation": 512

Networking Modes

VERY important.

bridge

Traditional Docker bridge network.

Mostly EC2 mode.

host

Container shares host networking.

High performance.

Less isolation.

awsvpc

MOST IMPORTANT modern mode.

Each task gets:

Dedicated ENI + private IP

Required for Fargate.

Example

Task A → 10.0.1.5
Task B → 10.0.1.9

Strong isolation.

Task Role vs Execution Role

VERY important interview topic.

Execution Role

Used by ECS itself.

Example:

  • Pull image from ECR
  • Send logs

Task Role

Used by your application.

Example:

  • Read S3
  • Access DynamoDB

Example

Execution Role
 └── ECS infrastructure permissions

Task Role
 └── Application permissions

Volumes

Tasks may define storage.

Ephemeral Storage

Temporary.

Destroyed when task stops.

Shared Volumes

Containers inside same task can share files.

Example:

App container
↕
Log container

EFS Integration

Persistent network storage.

Example:

"efsVolumeConfiguration": {}

Useful for:

  • Shared uploads
  • ML models
  • Persistent files

Multi-container Task Example

Production-style example:

Task
 ├── API Container
 ├── Nginx Container
 └── FluentBit Container

Why Multiple Containers?

Example responsibilities:

ContainerResponsibility
APIBusiness logic
NginxReverse proxy
FluentBitLog forwarding

Sidecar Containers

Common production pattern.

Main App + helper container

Examples:

  • Logging
  • Monitoring
  • Security agent
  • Metrics exporter

ECS Task Definition vs Docker Compose

Very important.

Similar idea.

Docker Compose

services:
  api:
    image: my-api

ECS Task Definition

AWS production-oriented equivalent.

Deployment Flow

Build Docker Image
      ↓
Push to ECR
      ↓
Create new task definition revision
      ↓
Update ECS Service
      ↓
Rolling deployment starts

Common Beginner Mistakes

Mistake 1

Thinking task definition runs containers.

Wrong.

It is ONLY blueprint.

Mistake 2

Editing old revision.

Wrong.

Create new revision.

Mistake 3

Hardcoding secrets.

Use:

  • Secrets Manager
  • Parameter Store
  • Task Roles

Mistake 4

Confusing task role and execution role.

Very common interview question.

Real Production Example

backend-api:14
 ├── Node.js container
 ├── CloudWatch logs
 ├── Health checks
 ├── Task role
 ├── awsvpc networking
 └── Secrets Manager integration

Production Best Practices

Use Immutable Revisions

Never mutate running configs.

Use awsvpc Mode

Modern standard.

Use Health Checks

Mandatory.

Use Secrets Manager

Avoid plaintext secrets.

Keep Containers Stateless

Do not store important data locally.

ECS Task Definition vs Kubernetes Pod Spec

Closest equivalent:

ECSKubernetes
Task DefinitionPod Spec
TaskPod

Interview Question

Question

Why are task definition revisions important?

Answer

Because deployments must be:

  • Versioned
  • Reproducible
  • Rollback-safe

Deep Mental Model

Task Definition
   = Recipe

Task
   = Cooked food

Service
   = Restaurant manager

3.5 ECS agents

3.5 ECS Agents

What is ECS Agent

ECS Agent is:

A software process running on ECS container instances that communicates with the ECS control plane.

Very simplified:

ECS Agent = Bridge between AWS ECS and your server

Why ECS Agent Exists

AWS ECS itself does NOT directly control your EC2 machine.

Instead:

ECS Control Plane
        ↕
     ECS Agent
        ↕
 Docker / Container Runtime

Agent acts as communicator.

Main Responsibilities of ECS Agent

The ECS Agent:

  • Receives instructions from ECS
  • Starts containers
  • Stops containers
  • Reports task status
  • Reports health checks
  • Reports resource usage
  • Registers EC2 instance into cluster
  • Sends logs/metrics metadata

Real Workflow

Suppose you deploy new service.

Step 1

You tell ECS:

Run 3 backend tasks

Step 2

ECS Scheduler decides:

Run task on EC2 instance #5

Step 3

ECS Control Plane sends instruction:

Start this container

to ECS Agent on EC2.

Step 4

ECS Agent communicates with Docker:

docker pull image
docker run container

Step 5

Container starts.

Agent reports back:

Task is RUNNING

Architecture Deep View

AWS ECS Control Plane
        ↓
     ECS Agent
        ↓
Docker Engine
        ↓
Containers

Important Thing

ECS Agent exists mainly in:

EC2 Launch Type

because AWS must communicate with your EC2 machines.

What About Fargate?

In Fargate:

AWS manages infrastructure.

Agent still exists internally,

BUT:

You do not manage or see it.

AWS handles everything.

ECS Agent Runs as Container

Funny but important.

ECS Agent itself usually runs as Docker container.

Example:

docker ps

might show:

amazon/amazon-ecs-agent

ECS Agent Registration Process

When EC2 instance boots:

Step 1

ECS Agent starts.

Step 2

Agent reads cluster configuration.

Example:

ECS_CLUSTER=production-cluster

Step 3

Agent registers instance into cluster.

Step 4

Cluster now sees container instance.

Example:

Cluster
 └── Container Instance
       └── ECS Agent connected

Container Instance Reminder

Very important.

Container instance means:

EC2 instance registered into ECS cluster

NOT container.

ECS Agent and Docker

ECS Agent interacts with:

  • Docker daemon
  • containerd (newer systems)

Commands internally similar to:

docker pull
docker create
docker start
docker stop

ECS Agent Monitoring

Agent continuously monitors:

  • Running tasks
  • Container health
  • CPU usage
  • Memory usage
  • Task status

Then sends updates to ECS.

Example

Task crashed

Agent reports:

STOPPED

ECS Service then launches replacement.

ECS Agent Heartbeats

Agent regularly sends heartbeat messages.

Purpose:

Tell ECS:
"I'm alive"

If Agent Disconnects

Example:

EC2 crashed
Network issue
Agent frozen

ECS marks container instance unhealthy.

Tasks may be rescheduled elsewhere.

ECS Agent Configuration

Agent configurable using environment variables.

Usually:

/etc/ecs/ecs.config

Example Config

ECS_CLUSTER=production-cluster
ECS_LOGLEVEL=info

Common ECS Agent Settings

VariablePurpose
ECS_CLUSTERCluster name
ECS_LOGLEVELLogging verbosity
ECS_ENABLE_TASK_IAM_ROLEEnable task IAM roles
ECS_AVAILABLE_LOGGING_DRIVERSSupported log drivers

ECS Optimized AMI

AWS provides special ECS-ready AMIs.

These include:

  • ECS Agent preinstalled
  • Docker preconfigured
  • ECS integration ready

Very common production choice.

Example

Amazon Machine Image

optimized for ECS:

Amazon ECS-Optimized AMI

Why ECS Optimized AMI Matters

Without it:

You manually install:

  • Docker
  • ECS Agent
  • Configurations

Optimized AMI simplifies everything.

ECS Agent Logs

Very important for debugging.

Common log location:

/var/log/ecs/ecs-agent.log

Example Problems

You check logs if:

  • Tasks not starting
  • Agent disconnected
  • Image pull failed
  • IAM issues
  • Networking problems

ECS Agent Update

AWS periodically updates ECS Agent.

Updates may include:

  • Bug fixes
  • Security fixes
  • New ECS features

Why Updates Matter

Old agent versions may not support:

  • New task definition features
  • Fargate features
  • IAM improvements
  • New networking modes

ECS Agent and IAM Roles

Agent uses EC2 instance IAM role.

Example permissions:

ecs:RegisterContainerInstance
ecs:SubmitTaskStateChange
ecs:Poll

Without permissions:

Agent cannot communicate with ECS

ECS Agent vs Task Role

VERY important distinction.

ECS Agent Uses

EC2 Instance Role

for ECS infrastructure communication.

Application Uses

Task Role

for app AWS access.

Example

ECS Agent
 └── Uses EC2 IAM Role

App Container
 └── Uses Task IAM Role

ECS Agent and Task Placement

Agent reports available resources:

Example:

CPU free
Memory free
Ports available

Scheduler uses this information.

Example

Suppose EC2 instance has:

8GB RAM total
6GB used
2GB free

Agent reports:

2GB available

Scheduler decides whether task fits.

ECS Agent and Health Checks

Agent monitors:

  • Container health
  • Docker status
  • Exit codes

Example:

Container exited with code 1

Agent reports failure.

ECS Agent and Networking

Agent helps configure:

  • ENIs
  • awsvpc networking
  • Task networking

Especially important in:

awsvpc mode

ECS Anywhere

Interesting advanced feature.

ECS Agent can run outside AWS.

Example:

On-premise servers
Other cloud providers

Using:

Amazon ECS Anywhere

ECS Agent Failure Scenario

Suppose:

Agent stops running

Then:

  • ECS loses communication
  • Tasks may appear unhealthy
  • New deployments fail
  • Monitoring breaks

VERY critical component.

Common Beginner Mistakes

Mistake 1

Thinking ECS directly controls Docker.

Wrong.

ECS communicates THROUGH ECS Agent.

Mistake 2

Confusing ECS Agent with app container.

Agent is infrastructure component.

Mistake 3

Ignoring ECS Agent version.

Old versions cause weird issues.

ECS Agent vs Kubernetes Kubelet

VERY important comparison.

ECSKubernetes
ECS AgentKubelet

Both:

  • Run on worker nodes
  • Manage containers
  • Talk to orchestration control plane

Deep Internal Flow

ECS Service
      ↓
ECS Scheduler
      ↓
ECS Agent
      ↓
Docker Runtime
      ↓
Containers

Production Best Practices

Use ECS Optimized AMIs

Avoid manual setup.

Keep Agent Updated

Prevent compatibility issues.

Monitor Agent Health

Critical infrastructure component.

Check Logs During Issues

Very important debugging step.

Interview Question

Question

What is the role of ECS Agent in ECS architecture?

Answer

ECS Agent:

  • Runs on ECS container instances
  • Communicates with ECS control plane
  • Starts/stops containers
  • Reports health and status
  • Manages task lifecycle on EC2 machines

Real Mental Model

ECS Control Plane
   = Brain

ECS Agent
   = Messenger + executor

Docker
   = Actual container engine

3.6 ECS scheduler

3.6 ECS Scheduler

What is ECS Scheduler

ECS Scheduler is:

The component responsible for deciding where and how ECS tasks should run.

Very simplified:

Scheduler = Decision maker

Main Responsibility

Scheduler answers questions like:

Which server should run this task?
Can this task fit there?
Should task be restarted?
Should tasks be spread across AZs?

Why Scheduler Exists

Imagine:

100 EC2 instances
1000 tasks
Different CPU/memory requirements
Multiple availability zones
Different placement rules

Manually deciding placement would be impossible.

Scheduler automates this.

Core Idea

Scheduler tries to match:

Desired State

with:

Actual Infrastructure State

Example

Desired:

Run 5 backend tasks

Actual:

Only 3 tasks running

Scheduler detects mismatch and launches 2 more tasks.

Scheduler Architecture

ECS Service
      ↓
ECS Scheduler
      ↓
ECS Agent
      ↓
Docker Runtime

Scheduler Inputs

Scheduler considers MANY things before placement.

1. CPU Availability

Example:

Task requires:
1 vCPU

Scheduler checks available CPU.

2. Memory Availability

Example:

Task needs 2GB RAM

Scheduler ensures machine has enough memory.

3. Port Availability

If using EC2 + host networking:

Port 4000 already occupied?

4. Placement Constraints

Rules restricting placement.

Example:

Run only in specific AZ
Run only on GPU instances

5. Placement Strategies

How tasks should be distributed.

6. Health Status

Avoid unhealthy instances.

7. Capacity Providers

Determines infrastructure source.

Example:

Fargate
Fargate Spot
Specific EC2 ASG

Scheduler Types

There are mainly two scheduling models in ECS.

1. Service Scheduler

Used for long-running services.

Example:

Backend API
Auth Service
Payment Service

Scheduler continuously maintains desired count.

Example

Desired Count = 3

If one task dies:

Scheduler launches replacement

2. Standalone Task Scheduler

Used for one-time/manual tasks.

Example:

Migration job
Cron task
Data processing job

Task runs once.

No continuous maintenance.

Scheduling Flow

Step 1

Service says:

Need 4 tasks

Step 2

Scheduler analyzes cluster state.

Checks:

  • CPU
  • Memory
  • Networking
  • Constraints
  • Availability

Step 3

Scheduler selects target infrastructure.

Example:

EC2 instance #12

or:

Fargate infrastructure

Step 4

Scheduler sends instruction to ECS Agent.

Step 5

Agent starts task.

Scheduler in EC2 Launch Type

Scheduler must decide:

Which EC2 instance should run task?

Very important because infrastructure is limited.

Example

Suppose cluster contains:

InstanceFree CPUFree RAM
EC2-A2 vCPU4GB
EC2-B0.5 vCPU1GB
EC2-C4 vCPU8GB

Task requires:

1 vCPU
2GB RAM

Scheduler may choose:

EC2-A or EC2-C

NOT EC2-B.

Scheduler in Fargate

Simpler.

AWS manages infrastructure automatically.

Scheduler mainly validates:

  • Task configuration
  • Capacity provider
  • Networking

Then AWS provisions runtime.

Placement Constraints

Hard rules.

Example Constraint

Only run in us-east-1a

or:

Only run on GPU instances

Example EC2 Attribute

ecs.instance-type == g4dn.xlarge

Used for ML workloads.

Placement Strategies

Defines HOW scheduler distributes tasks.

1. Spread Strategy

Distribute tasks evenly.

Example:

Across Availability Zones
Across EC2 instances

Example

AZ-1 → 2 tasks
AZ-2 → 2 tasks

Improves availability.

2. Binpack Strategy

Pack tasks tightly.

Goal:

Use minimum servers possible

Cost optimization.

Example

Instead of:

4 servers partially used

scheduler prefers:

2 servers highly utilized

3. Random Strategy

Random placement.

Rarely used in production.

Scheduler and Availability Zones

Very important for HA.

Scheduler tries distributing tasks across AZs.

Example:

Task 1 → AZ-A
Task 2 → AZ-B
Task 3 → AZ-C

If one AZ fails:

Application still alive

Scheduler and Resource Reservation

Scheduler prevents over-allocation.

Example:

EC2 instance:

8GB RAM total

Tasks already use:

7GB

New task needs:

2GB

Scheduler rejects placement.

Scheduler and Health Checks

Scheduler reacts to unhealthy tasks.

Example:

Task failed ALB health check

Scheduler:

Stops task
Launches replacement

Scheduler and Auto Scaling

Scheduler works closely with scaling systems.

Example:

CPU > 70%

Auto Scaling says:

Need more tasks

Scheduler places new tasks.

Scheduler and Capacity Providers

Scheduler chooses infrastructure source.

Example:

70% Fargate
30% Fargate Spot

Scheduler distributes tasks accordingly.

Scheduler Failure Handling

Suppose:

EC2 instance crashes

Scheduler detects lost tasks.

Then:

Reschedules tasks elsewhere

Very important self-healing behavior.

Scheduler and Rolling Deployments

During deployment:

Old tasks removed gradually
New tasks launched gradually

Scheduler coordinates transition.

Example Deployment Flow

Task v1
      ↓
Task v2 launched
      ↓
Health check passes
      ↓
Old v1 task removed

Scheduler and Draining

When EC2 instance must be removed:

Container instance → DRAINING

Scheduler stops placing new tasks there.

Existing tasks migrate away safely.

Scheduler and Stateful Workloads

ECS Scheduler works BEST with:

Stateless applications

because tasks can move freely.

ECS Scheduler vs Kubernetes Scheduler

Very important comparison.

ECSKubernetes
ECS Schedulerkube-scheduler

Both:

  • Decide placement
  • Match resources
  • Handle constraints
  • Optimize distribution

Common Beginner Mistakes

Mistake 1

Thinking scheduler only starts tasks once.

Wrong.

Scheduler continuously monitors cluster state.

Mistake 2

Ignoring placement strategies.

Can cause:

  • Bad HA
  • Uneven load
  • Higher costs

Mistake 3

Confusing ECS Agent with Scheduler.

ComponentRole
SchedulerMakes decisions
ECS AgentExecutes decisions

Real Production Example

Cluster:
- 20 EC2 instances
- 5 services
- 100 running tasks

Scheduler continuously:
- Places tasks
- Replaces failed tasks
- Balances AZs
- Optimizes capacity

Deep Internal Flow

Desired State
      ↓
Scheduler
      ↓
Placement Decision
      ↓
ECS Agent
      ↓
Container Runtime
      ↓
Running Task

Production Best Practices

Use Spread Across AZs

High availability.

Use Binpack Carefully

Good for cost optimization.

Configure Constraints Properly

Avoid bad placements.

Monitor Resource Utilization

Prevent scheduling failures.

Interview Question

Question

What is the role of ECS Scheduler?

Answer

ECS Scheduler:

  • Determines where tasks should run
  • Matches resource requirements
  • Applies placement constraints/strategies
  • Maintains desired task count
  • Replaces failed tasks
  • Supports deployments and scaling

Real Mental Model

Scheduler
   = Smart dispatcher

ECS Agent
   = Worker executing commands

Task
   = Actual workload

3.7 Capacity providers

3.7 Capacity Providers

What are Capacity Providers

Capacity Providers define:

Where ECS tasks should run.

Very simplified:

Capacity Provider = Infrastructure source for tasks

Why They Exist

Before capacity providers, ECS users manually managed:

  • EC2 scaling
  • Infrastructure selection
  • Task placement logic

Capacity providers simplify this.

Main Types

ECS mainly supports:

TypeDescription
FargateServerless containers
Fargate SpotCheap interruptible Fargate
EC2 Auto Scaling GroupYour EC2 infrastructure

1. Fargate Capacity Provider

AWS fully manages infrastructure.

You only define:

  • CPU
  • Memory
  • Container image

Best for:

  • Simplicity
  • Microservices
  • Small/medium apps

Example

Task
 └── Runs on AWS-managed server

No EC2 management.

2. Fargate Spot

Same as Fargate BUT cheaper.

Uses spare AWS capacity.

Important

Tasks MAY suddenly stop if AWS needs capacity.

Best for:

  • Background jobs
  • Workers
  • Non-critical workloads

NOT ideal for critical APIs.

Example

70% cheaper
BUT interruptible

3. EC2 Capacity Provider

Uses your own EC2 Auto Scaling Group.

You manage:

  • EC2 types
  • Scaling
  • Patching
  • Infrastructure

Best for:

  • Large-scale systems
  • GPU workloads
  • Cost optimization
  • Special infrastructure needs

Architecture

ECS Cluster
   ↓
Capacity Provider
   ↓
EC2 Auto Scaling Group
   ↓
EC2 Instances

Capacity Provider Strategy

VERY important concept.

It defines:

How tasks should distribute across providers

Example

80% Fargate
20% Fargate Spot

ECS distributes tasks automatically.

Base and Weight

Capacity provider strategies use:

PropertyMeaning
BaseMinimum tasks
WeightRelative distribution

Example

Fargate:
  Base = 2
  Weight = 1

Fargate Spot:
  Weight = 4

Meaning:

  • First 2 tasks always on Fargate
  • Remaining tasks distributed mostly to Spot

Real Production Example

Critical API Tasks
   → Fargate

Background Workers
   → Fargate Spot

Optimizes cost + reliability.

Capacity Providers and Auto Scaling

For EC2 providers:

Capacity provider integrates with:

Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling

Automatically:

  • Launches EC2 instances
  • Removes unused instances
  • Balances capacity

Example Flow

More ECS tasks needed
      ↓
Not enough EC2 capacity
      ↓
Auto Scaling Group launches new EC2
      ↓
ECS places tasks there

Managed Scaling

ECS can automatically scale EC2 capacity.

This is called:

Managed Scaling

AWS adjusts infrastructure automatically.

Managed Termination Protection

Prevents ECS from accidentally terminating EC2 instances that still run important tasks.

Very useful in production.

Capacity Provider vs Cluster

Important distinction:

ComponentRole
ClusterLogical environment
Capacity ProviderInfrastructure source

ECS Capacity Provider vs Kubernetes Node Groups

Closest Kubernetes equivalent:

ECSKubernetes
Capacity ProviderNode Group

Common Beginner Recommendation

For learning/small apps:

Use Fargate

For advanced optimization later:

Use EC2 Capacity Providers

Common Beginner Mistakes

Mistake 1

Thinking capacity provider runs containers.

Wrong.

It only provides infrastructure.

Mistake 2

Using only Fargate Spot for critical systems.

Spot tasks may disappear unexpectedly.

Mistake 3

Confusing cluster with capacity provider.

Cluster = organization.

Capacity provider = compute source.

Interview Question

Question

What problem do ECS Capacity Providers solve?

Answer

They simplify infrastructure management and allow ECS tasks to run on different compute sources like:

  • Fargate
  • Fargate Spot
  • EC2 Auto Scaling Groups

with automatic scaling and placement strategies.

4. ECS Launch Types

ECS Launch Types

Launch Type defines:

What infrastructure will run your ECS tasks.

Very simplified:

Launch Type = Runtime environment for containers

Main ECS Launch Types

Launch TypeInfrastructure
EC2Your EC2 instances
FargateAWS-managed serverless infrastructure
ExternalOn-premise or external servers

1. EC2 Launch Type

Tasks run on:

Amazon EC2 instances that YOU manage.

Architecture:

ECS Cluster
   ↓
EC2 Instances
   ↓
Docker Containers

You Manage

  • EC2 sizing
  • OS updates
  • Docker
  • ECS Agent
  • Scaling
  • Patching

Advantages

AdvantageExplanation
Full controlComplete infrastructure access
Cheaper at scaleBetter long-term cost
GPU supportAI/ML workloads
Custom AMIsSpecialized setups

Disadvantages

ProblemExplanation
Operational overheadMore DevOps work
Capacity planningMust manage servers
Scaling complexityNeed ASGs

  • Large-scale systems
  • GPU workloads
  • Advanced networking
  • Cost optimization

2. Fargate Launch Type

Serverless containers.

AWS manages infrastructure completely.

Architecture:

ECS Cluster
   ↓
AWS-managed infrastructure
   ↓
Containers

You Only Configure

  • CPU
  • Memory
  • Image
  • Networking

AWS handles everything else.

Advantages

AdvantageExplanation
No server managementHuge simplicity
Fast setupMinimal ops
Auto infrastructureAWS handles scaling
Strong isolationTask-level isolation

Disadvantages

ProblemExplanation
More expensiveCompared to EC2

  • APIs
  • Microservices
  • Startups
  • Small/medium systems

3. External Launch Type

Using:

Amazon ECS Anywhere

Examples:

  • On-premise servers
  • Other cloud providers

Comparison

FeatureEC2Fargate
Server managementYouAWS
SimplicityMediumVery easy
Cost at scaleCheaperMore expensive
ControlHighLimited
ScalingManual/ASGAutomatic
GPU supportYesLimited

Important Distinction

Many beginners confuse:

ConceptMeaning
Launch TypeWhere tasks run
Capacity ProviderStrategy/infrastructure provider

Relationship Between Them

Launch Type
   ↓
Defines runtime infrastructure

Capacity Provider
   ↓
Controls how infrastructure is supplied/scaled

Modern Recommendation

For learning and most modern apps:

ECS + Fargate

For advanced production optimization:

ECS + EC2

Interview Question

Question

What is the difference between ECS EC2 and Fargate launch types?

Answer

EC2 launch type requires managing your own EC2 infrastructure.

Fargate is serverless, where AWS manages infrastructure automatically.

4.2 Fargate launch type

4.2 Fargate Launch Type

What is Fargate

AWS Fargate is a serverless compute engine for containers.

Very simplified:

Fargate = Run containers without managing servers

Traditional Problem

Normally with containers you must manage:

  • EC2 instances
  • OS updates
  • Docker installation
  • Scaling servers
  • Capacity planning
  • Infrastructure monitoring

Fargate removes all of this.

Main Idea

You only define:

- CPU
- Memory
- Docker image
- Networking

AWS handles:

- Servers
- Scaling infrastructure
- Runtime
- Patching
- Availability

Architecture

Traditional EC2 ECS:

You
 ↓
Manage EC2
 ↓
Run containers

Fargate:

You
 ↓
Define task
 ↓
AWS runs it automatically

Real Workflow

Step 1

Create Docker image.

Example:

docker build -t backend-api .

Step 2

Push image to:

Amazon Elastic Container Registry

Step 3

Create ECS Task Definition.

Example:

CPU: 512
Memory: 1024
Port: 4000

Step 4

Create ECS Service using:

Launch Type = FARGATE

Step 5

AWS automatically provisions infrastructure.

Container starts running.

What You DO NOT Manage

With Fargate you NEVER manage:

  • EC2 instances
  • ECS agent
  • Docker daemon
  • OS patches
  • Infrastructure scaling
  • Server failures

This is why it is called:

Serverless containers

Fargate Internals

Even though you don't see servers:

Containers STILL run on servers internally

AWS simply hides and manages them for you.

Fargate Networking

VERY important.

Fargate requires:

awsvpc network mode

Meaning:

Each task gets its own ENI and private IP

Example

Task A → 10.0.1.5
Task B → 10.0.1.8

Tasks behave almost like mini virtual machines.

Strong Isolation

One huge advantage.

Each Fargate task has strong isolation between workloads.

Better security compared to shared EC2 hosts.

Resource Configuration

You define:

  • CPU
  • Memory

Example:

0.5 vCPU
1GB RAM

AWS allocates required infrastructure automatically.

Supported CPU/Memory Combinations

Fargate only allows valid combinations.

Example:

CPUAllowed Memory
256512MB–2GB
5121GB–4GB
10242GB–8GB

Fargate Scaling

Very easy.

ECS simply launches more tasks.

Example:

2 Tasks
→
10 Tasks

No server management needed.

High Availability

Fargate tasks can automatically spread across:

  • Availability Zones
  • Subnets

Example:

AZ-A → 2 tasks
AZ-B → 2 tasks

Fargate Pricing

You pay for:

  • CPU
  • Memory
  • Runtime duration

NOT for EC2 instances.

Important Difference

EC2 pricing:

Pay for server even if idle

Fargate pricing:

Pay per running task resources

Fargate Spot

Cheaper version of Fargate.

Uses spare AWS capacity.

Can be interrupted.

Best for:

  • Workers
  • Batch jobs
  • Non-critical workloads

Common Use Cases

Fargate is VERY popular for:

Use CaseWhy
APIsSimple deployment
MicroservicesEasy scaling
Background workersFast setup
StartupsLow operational overhead
Internal toolsMinimal DevOps

Logging

Usually integrated with:

Amazon CloudWatch

Example:

Container logs
→ CloudWatch Logs

IAM Integration

Fargate tasks support:

Task IAM Roles

Your app can securely access:

  • S3
  • SQS
  • DynamoDB
  • Secrets Manager

without hardcoded credentials.

Storage

By default:

Ephemeral storage

Meaning:

Data disappears when task stops

For persistence use:

  • S3
  • RDS
  • EFS

Fargate vs EC2

FeatureFargateEC2
Server managementAWSYou
SimplicityVery highMedium
Cost efficiency at scaleLowerHigher
ControlLimitedFull
Operational overheadVery lowHigher

Limitations of Fargate

Less Host Control

Cannot:

  • SSH into host
  • Customize kernel
  • Install host software

More Expensive

Usually more expensive than EC2 at very large scale.

Some Advanced Features Limited

Compared to EC2:

  • GPU support
  • Deep networking customization
  • Specialized workloads

Best Practice Recommendation

For most modern applications:

Start with Fargate

Then optimize later if needed.

Common Beginner Mistakes

Mistake 1

Thinking Fargate has no servers at all.

Wrong.

AWS manages hidden infrastructure.

Mistake 2

Trying to SSH into Fargate.

No direct host access.

Mistake 3

Storing important data inside container filesystem.

Containers are ephemeral.

Real Production Architecture

Users
   ↓
Application Load Balancer
   ↓
ECS Service
   ↓
Fargate Tasks
   ↓
RDS / Redis / S3

Interview Question

Question

What problem does AWS Fargate solve?

Answer

Fargate removes the need to manage container infrastructure like EC2 servers, Docker hosts, and scaling, allowing developers to run containers in a serverless way.

Mental Model

EC2 ECS
   = You manage restaurant building

Fargate
   = AWS owns building, you only cook food

1. Introduction to ECR
1.1 What is ECR

1.1 What is Amazon ECR?

ECR (Elastic Container Registry) is an AWS service that stores and manages Docker container images.

Think:

Source Code
   ↓
docker build
   ↓
Docker Image
   ↓
Push to ECR
   ↓
ECS / EC2 / Lambda pulls image
   ↓
Application runs

ECR itself does not run containers.

Its only responsibility is:

  • Store images
  • Version images
  • Secure images
  • Deliver images to compute services

Why ECR Exists

Imagine you built this:

NestJS Backend
React Frontend
Postgres

You create:

docker build-t backend .

Now you have:

backend:latest

Question:

Where do you store it?

Options:

  • Docker Hub
  • GitHub Registry
  • AWS ECR ← AWS solution

ECR is AWS's answer.

Real Production Flow

Imagine your CRM project.

You write:

NestJS
↓
docker build
↓
backend:v1
↓
docker push ECR
↓
ECS pulls
↓
Container starts

You never upload:

app.ts
controller.ts
service.ts

You upload:

Entire packaged environment

Inside image:

Node
NestJS
Dependencies
Built app
Configs

Core Components

1. Registry

Top-level storage.

Example:

AWS Account
└── Registry

One registry per region/account.

Example:

123456789.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com

2. Repository

Folder for images.

Example:

backend
frontend
payment-service

Repository:

backend

Contains:

backend:v1
backend:v2
backend:latest

3. Image

Actual deployable package.

Example:

backend:v2

Contains:

Linux
Node
node_modules
dist/

Important Distinction

Many beginners confuse this.

Dockerfile
≠
Docker Image
≠
Container

Dockerfile

Instructions.

FROM node:22
COPY .
RUN npm install

↓

Docker Image

Built artifact.

backend:v1

↓

Container

Running process.

Container ID

ECR in AWS Ecosystem

Code
 ↓
CodeBuild / GitHub Actions
 ↓
Docker Build
 ↓
ECR
 ↓
ECS
 ↓
ALB
 ↓
Users

Very Important (Interview Level)

If interviewer asks:

"What is ECR?"

Good answer:

ECR is AWS managed container registry used to store, version and distribute container images. Services like ECS, EKS, EC2 and Lambda can pull images from ECR and run containers.

One line to remember

ECR stores images. ECS runs images.
1.2 Why ECR Exists

Perfect. This section is where ECR starts making sense.

1.2 Why ECR Exists

Question:

Docker can already build images. Why do we need ECR?

Because Docker builds images locally but does not solve centralized storage and deployment.

Problem Without ECR

Imagine your project.

You build:

docker build -t backend:v1 .

Now image exists only here:

Muzaffar's MacBook

Question:

How will ECS in AWS get this image?

It cannot.

Problem 1 — Images stay local

Without registry:

Laptop
└── backend:v1

Production server:

❌ cannot access

Need:

Laptop
 ↓
Push
 ↓
Central Storage
 ↓
Server Pull

That storage is:

ECR

Problem 2 — Multiple Servers Need Same Image

Imagine:

ECS Service
 ├── Task 1
 ├── Task 2
 ├── Task 3

All need:

backend:v5

Without registry:

copy manually ❌

With ECR:

Task 1 → Pull
Task 2 → Pull
Task 3 → Pull

Same image.

Problem 3 — Version Management

Imagine:

backend:v1
backend:v2
backend:v3

Production currently:

v2

New deployment:

v3

Bug appears.

Rollback:

v2

Registry enables:

store
version
rollback

Problem 4 — CI/CD Needs Shared Storage

Imagine GitHub Actions.

Developer:

git push

Pipeline:

Build Docker Image
↓
Push ECR
↓
Deploy ECS

Without ECR:

CI builds image
but nowhere to store

Problem 5 — ECS Needs Pull Source

Remember yesterday.

Task Definition:

{
 "image":
 "123.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/backend:v2"
}

ECS does:

Start Task
↓
Read image
↓
Download image
↓
Run container

Without ECR:

No image
No container

Problem 6 — Security

ECR integrates with:

  • IAM
  • VPC
  • Encryption
  • Vulnerability scanning

Example:

Developer
   ↓
Push Allowed

Random User
   ↓
Access Denied

Real Flow

Without ECR:

Mac
↓
docker build
↓
???
↓
Production

Broken.

With ECR:

Mac
↓
docker build
↓
docker push
↓
ECR
↓
ECS pull
↓
Container running

Simple Analogy

Docker → creates movie

ECR → Netflix storage

ECS → TV that plays movie

Interview Question

Why not upload source code directly to ECS?

Answer:

Because ECS runs containers, not source code. Source code must first be packaged into Docker images and stored in ECR.

One sentence to remember

Docker creates images. ECR distributes images. ECS executes images.

1.3 ECR vs Docker Hub (this one is important because interviewers love asking it).

1.3 ECR vs Docker Hub

Good. This one is interview-favorite because people often think:

Docker Hub = ECR

Not exactly.

1.3 ECR vs Docker Hub

First understand:

Both do the same high-level job:

Store Docker images.

But they are optimized for different ecosystems.

Quick Comparison

FeatureECRDocker Hub
OwnerAWSDocker
PurposeAWS container registryGeneral container registry
AuthenticationIAMDocker accounts
ECS IntegrationNativeManual
EKS IntegrationNativeManual
Private reposStrong supportSupported
Image scanningBuilt-inAvailable
Network speed in AWSUsually betterExternal
PricingPay for storage/usageFree + paid tiers
Production AWS usageVery commonCommon but less AWS-native

Mental Model

Docker Hub

Like:

GitHub

Public place.

Anyone can publish images.

Example:

docker pull node
docker pull postgres
docker pull nginx

Those usually come from Docker Hub.

ECR

Like:

Private company GitHub
inside AWS

Store your production images.

Example:

crm-backend:v1
payment-service:v4
frontend:v12

Architecture Comparison

Docker Hub

Developer
 ↓
docker push
 ↓
Docker Hub
 ↓
AWS ECS
 ↓
pull image

External dependency.

ECR

Developer
 ↓
docker push
 ↓
ECR
 ↓
ECS
 ↓
run

Everything stays inside AWS.

Example

You create image:

docker build -t backend:v1 .

Push to Docker Hub:

docker push muzaffar/backend:v1

Image:

docker.io/muzaffar/backend:v1

Push to ECR:

docker push \
123456.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/backend:v1

Image:

123456.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/backend:v1

Authentication Difference

Docker Hub

Login:

docker login

Uses:

username
password
token

ECR

Login:

aws ecr get-login-password

Uses:

IAM
AWS credentials
roles

This becomes powerful in ECS.

Example:

ECS Task Role
↓
Pull ECR
↓
No password stored

Production Example

Your future deployment:

GitHub
 ↓
GitHub Actions
 ↓
Build Docker Image
 ↓
Push ECR
 ↓
ECS Deploy
 ↓
ALB
 ↓
Users

You usually will not insert Docker Hub here.

So why does Docker Hub still exist?

Because AWS is not always used.

Examples:

Local Development
Open Source
Learning
Multi-cloud

People often pull:

node
mongo
redis
postgres

from Docker Hub.

When to Choose What

Choose Docker Hub when:

✅ Learning

✅ Public images

✅ Open source

Choose ECR when:

✅ ECS

✅ EKS

✅ Production AWS

✅ Private deployments

Interview Question

If ECS can pull from Docker Hub, why use ECR?

Answer:

Because ECR provides tighter AWS integration, IAM security, easier deployments, lower operational overhead, and optimized access from AWS services.

One sentence to remember

Docker Hub is general storage for container images. ECR is AWS-native storage for container images.

1.4 Where ECR Fits Inside AWS Architecture

Perfect. This is the section that connects yesterday’s ECS learning with today’s ECR.

1.4 Where ECR Fits Inside AWS Architecture

Question:

We learned ECS yesterday.

We learned ECR today.

Now where exactly does ECR sit?

Short answer:

ECR sits between Build and Deployment.

High-Level AWS Deployment Flow

Developer
   ↓
Write Code
   ↓
Build Docker Image
   ↓
ECR
   ↓
ECS
   ↓
Load Balancer
   ↓
Users

Meaning:

Code
→ Package
→ Store
→ Execute
→ Serve

Real AWS Architecture

Browser
   ↓
ALB
(Application Load Balancer)
   ↓
ECS Service
   ↓
ECS Tasks
   ↓
Containers
   ↑
Pull Images
   ↑
ECR

Notice:

ECR is not in request path.

Users never talk to ECR.

Request Path vs Deployment Path

This distinction is VERY important.

Runtime Request Flow

(User traffic)

User
 ↓
Load Balancer
 ↓
Container
 ↓
Database

No ECR.

Deployment Flow

(New release)

Developer
 ↓
docker build
 ↓
docker push
 ↓
ECR
 ↓
ECS deploy
 ↓
Task pulls image
 ↓
Container starts

ECR appears here.

Let's Follow a Real Deployment

Imagine your CRM.

You changed:

UsersController

and push code.

Step 1 — Build

docker build -t crm:v5 .

Produces:

crm:v5

Step 2 — Store

docker push ECR

Now:

ECR
└── crm:v5

Step 3 — Deploy

ECS Service updates.

Task Definition:

{
 "image":
 "ecr/crm:v5"
}

Step 4 — Pull

Task starts.

ECS Agent
↓
Call ECR
↓
Download image
↓
Start container

Step 5 — Serve Traffic

Now:

User
↓
ALB
↓
ECS
↓
Container(v5)

Again:

No ECR.

Because image is already downloaded.

ECR Relationships with AWS Services

2. Core ECR Concepts

These are the 5 things you must know:

Registry
 ↓

AWS Account
 ↓
Registry
 ↓
Repository

 ↓

2.1 Registry

Top-level container storage.

Think:

GitHub Account

but for images.

Inside AWS account:

AWS Account
└── ECR Registry

Example:

123456789.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com

Breakdown:

123456789
↓
AWS account

dkr.ecr
↓
ECR service

us-east-1
↓
region

One registry usually exists per:

Account + Region

Example:

Account A
├── us-east-1 Registry
└── eu-central-1 Registry

Inside registry:

backend
frontend
payment

2.2 Repository

Repository is a folder for images.

Example:

backend

Contains:

backend:v1
backend:v2
backend:latest

Structure:

Registry
└── Repository

Example:

123.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com
└── backend

Repositories usually represent:

One service

Example microservices:

backend
users-service
payments-service
notification-service

Question:

Can repository contain containers?

Answer:

❌ No

Only images.

2.3 Image

Image = deployable package.

Contains:

OS
Runtime
Dependencies
Application
Configs

Example:

backend:v1

Created by:

docker build

Example:

docker build -t backend:v1 .

Produces:

Image

Image is:

READ ONLY

When running:

Image
↓
Container

Example:

backend:v1
↓
Container A

backend:v1
↓
Container B

Multiple containers can run from one image.

2.4 Tags

Tag = image version label.

Example:

backend:v1

Here:

backend
↓
repository

v1
↓
tag

Examples:

backend:v1
backend:v2
backend:v3
backend:latest

Production:

v5

Testing:

v6-beta

Bad practice:

latest

Good:

v1.0.3

Because:

latest

changes unexpectedly.

Real example:

docker tag \
backend:v1 \
123.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/backend:v1

2.5 Layers (VERY IMPORTANT)

This is where Docker becomes smart.

Image is not one giant file.

It is:

Image
├── Layer 1
├── Layer 2
├── Layer 3
└── Layer 4

Example Dockerfile:

FROM node:22

WORKDIR /app

COPY package.json .

RUN npm install

COPY . .

CMD ["npm","run","start"]

Creates:

Layer 1 → Node
Layer 2 → Workdir
Layer 3 → package.json
Layer 4 → npm install
Layer 5 → source code

Why layers matter?

Imagine:

Version 1:

backend:v1

Size:

700 MB

Change one file.

Build:

backend:v2

Without layers:

Upload 700 MB

With layers:

Upload only changed layer

Maybe:

20 MB

Huge optimization.

Real Pull Example

ECS:

Pull image

If layers exist:

Layer 1 → already exists
Layer 2 → already exists
Layer 3 → download

Fast deployment.

Visual Memory

Registry
└── Repository
     ├── Image:v1
     │     ├── Layer
     │     ├── Layer
     │     └── Layer
     │
     └── Image:v2

Interview Questions

Difference between Registry and Repository?

Registry:

Top storage

Repository:

Folder of images

Difference between Image and Container?

Image:

Blueprint

Container:

Running instance

Why layers?

Answer:

To reduce build and transfer time.

One line to remember

Registry stores repositories → repositories store images → images consist of layers → tags version images.
