3.1 Push Flow (Developer → ECR)

This is:

How images arrive into ECR.

Imagine you finished your NestJS feature.

Step 1 — Write Code

backend/
 ├── src
 ├── package.json
 └── Dockerfile

Step 2 — Build Image

Command:

docker build -t backend:v1 .

Docker:

Read Dockerfile
↓
Build layers
↓
Create image

Result:

backend:v1

Still local.

Step 3 — Authenticate to ECR

Example:

aws ecr get-login-password

Meaning:

AWS
↓
Verify IAM
↓
Allow docker push

Step 4 — Tag Image

Local:

backend:v1

Convert:

docker tag backend:v1 \
123.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/backend:v1

Now Docker understands destination.

Step 5 — Push

docker push \
123.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/backend:v1

Flow:

Laptop
↓
Compress layers
↓
Upload changed layers
↓
Store in ECR

Done.

Visual Push Flow

Developer
↓
docker build
↓
Local Image
↓
docker push
↓
ECR Repository

3.2 Pull Flow (ECS → ECR)

Now deployment starts.

Question:

How does ECS get containers?

Answer:

It downloads images.

Task Definition:

{
 "image":
 "123.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/backend:v1"
}

ECS Service
↓

↓
Task Starts

↓

↓

↓

Detailed:

ECS Scheduler
↓
Select EC2/Fargate
↓
ECS Agent
↓
docker pull
↓

Important:

ECS never downloads source code.

Only image.

ECR
↓
Pull Image
↓
ECS Task
↓
Container

3.3 Authentication Flow

Question:

Who gives permission?

Answer:

IAM.

Push:

Developer
↓
IAM User
↓

Permission:

ecr:PutImage

Pull:

ECS Task
↓
Task Execution Role
↓
ECR

Permission:

ecr:GetAuthorizationToken
ecr:BatchGetImage
ecr:GetDownloadUrlForLayer

Meaning:

Can download
Cannot push

Production:

GitHub Actions
↓
Assume Role
↓
Push ECR
↓
ECS Pull

Question:

Example:

Version 1:

├── v1

Delete others

5.1 How ECS Reads Image

Remember:

ECR only stores.

ECS runs.

Question:

How does ECS know which image to run?

Answer:

Task Definition

Task Definition contains:

{
 "containerDefinitions": [
   {
     "image":
"123456789.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/backend:v1"
   }
 ]
}

This line tells ECS:

Go to ECR
↓
Download backend:v1
↓
Run it

Architecture:

ECR
↓
Task Definition
↓
Task
↓
Container

5.2 Task Definition → ECR Connection

Yesterday we learned:

Task Definition is:

Blueprint of Task

Today add:

Task Definition also contains:

Image Location
CPU
Memory
Ports
Env
Volumes

Example:

{
 "family":"backend",

 "containerDefinitions":[
 {
  "name":"backend",

  "image":
"123456789.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/backend:v2",

  "cpu":512,

  "memory":1024,

  "portMappings":[
     {
       "containerPort":4000
     }
   ]
 }
 ]
}

Meaning:

backend:v2
↓
512 CPU
↓
1 GB RAM
↓
Port 4000

Task Definition is basically:

docker run
+
infra settings

This is VERY important.

or

↓

backend:v2

Step 5

Task Execution Role

↓

Step 6

Pull.

↓

Step 7

Start.

Visual:

Service
↓
Task
↓
Task Definition
↓
ECR
↓
Pull
↓
Container

What if Multiple Tasks Exist?

Example:

Desired Count = 3

Flow:

Task 1 → Pull v2
Task 2 → Pull v2
Task 3 → Pull v2

Same image.

Different containers.

Important Question

Does ECS pull every request?

No.

Wrong:

Request
↓
ECR

Correct:

Deploy
↓
Pull Once
↓
Run Container
↓
Serve Requests

6.1 Versioning Images

Question:

How do teams know which version is running?

Using tags.

Bad:

backend:latest

Good:

backend:v1
backend:v2
backend:v3

Even better:

backend:1.0.0
backend:1.0.1
backend:1.0.2

Production often:

backend:20260520-1340
backend:git-abc123

Example deployment:

Current:

backend:v12

Deploy:

backend:v13

Rollback:

backend:v12

No rebuild.

Typical strategy:

dev
staging
production

Example:

backend:dev
backend:staging
backend:v24

Real CI/CD Example

Git commit:

a7c9b2

Image:

backend:a7c9b2

Now deployment becomes traceable.

Production Rule

Avoid:

latest

Because:

today → image A
tomorrow → image B

Same tag.

Chaos.

6.2 Immutable Tags

Question:

Can someone overwrite backend:v5?

By default:

Sometimes yes

Danger.

Example:

Current:

backend:v5

Someone pushes:

backend:v5

again.

Now:

same tag
different image

Nightmare.

Solution:

Enable:

Tag Immutability

Result:

backend:v5

already exists →

Push Rejected

Must create:

backend:v6

Production usually:

Immutable = Enabled

Real deployment:

v1
v2
v3
v4

Never change history.

6.3 Image Scanning

Question:

What if image contains vulnerabilities?

Example:

Dockerfile:

FROM node:16

Imagine:

Old OpenSSL
Critical vulnerability

ECR can scan image.

Flow:

Push
↓
Scan
↓
Report

Example output:

HIGH → 2
MEDIUM → 5
LOW → 10

Meaning:

Update dependencies

Typical findings:

Old Ubuntu
Old Node
Old OpenSSL
Old Python

Production:

Scan On Push = Enabled

Important:

Scanning:

finds issues

It does NOT:

fix issues

6.4 Lifecycle Policies

Question:

What happens after 500 deployments?

Repository:

backend
├── v1
├── v2
├── v3
...
├── v500

Storage grows.

Costs grow.

Solution:

Lifecycle Policies.

Example:

Keep latest 10
Delete older

Result:

Before:

v1
v2
v3
...
v100

After:

v91
v92
...
v100

Example rule:

Delete untagged after 7 days

Useful because:

CI sometimes leaves:

sha1
sha2
sha3

unused.

Typical Production Rules

Rule 1:

Keep latest 20 images

Rule 2:

Delete untagged after 14 days

Rule 3:

Never delete production

Real Production Flow

Git Push
↓
Build
↓
Tag = commit hash
↓
Push ECR
↓
Scan
↓
Deploy ECS
↓
Lifecycle Cleanup

What Teams Usually Configure Immediately

Repository:

Private
Immutable Tags
Scan On Push
Lifecycle Enabled

Interview Questions

Why avoid latest?

Because same tag may point to different images.

Why immutable tags?

Prevent accidental overwrite.

Does scanning fix vulnerabilities?

No.

Only reports.

Why lifecycle?

Reduce storage and cost.

Production Checklist

✅ Version tags
✅ Immutable
✅ Scan enabled
✅ Lifecycle policy

One sentence to remember

Production ECR is mostly versioning, security, and cleanup.

ECR core is essentially complete.

2.What is API GATEWAY

Perfect. Now we start API Gateway properly.

1.1 What is API Gateway?

API Gateway is an AWS service that acts as the entry point (front door) for your backend APIs.

It receives requests and decides:

Where request goes
Who can access
How many requests allowed
How request is transformed

Short definition:

API Gateway receives HTTP requests and forwards them to backend services like Lambda, ECS, EC2, or AWS services.

First Understand the Problem

Imagine your backend.

Without API Gateway:

Users
 ↓
ECS
 ↓
Backend

User talks directly to backend.

With API Gateway:

Users
 ↓
API Gateway
 ↓
Backend

Gateway stands in front.

Real Example

Your CRM backend:

Endpoints:

POST /login
GET /courses
POST /invites

User request:

GET /courses

Flow:

Browser
↓
API Gateway
↓
Route Matching
↓
ECS
↓
Container
↓
Response

User never knows ECS exists.

Think of API Gateway as Reverse Proxy + API Manager

Responsibilities:

Receive
Validate
Route
Protect
Monitor
Respond

Internal View

API Gateway receives:

POST /users

Then:

Authenticate
↓
Apply Rate Limit
↓
Find Route
↓
Call Backend
↓
Return Response

Supported Backends

API Gateway can send requests to:

Lambda
ECS
EC2
ALB
AWS Services
HTTP APIs

Example:

POST /upload
↓
Lambda

GET /courses
↓
ECS

POST /payments
↓
EC2

Architecture Example — Lambda

Client
↓
API Gateway
↓
Lambda
↓
Response

Most serverless architecture uses this.

Architecture Example — ECS

Browser
↓
API Gateway
↓
ALB
↓
ECS
↓
Container

Very common.

Example Request

User:

GET /users

Gateway:

Match Route
↓
Forward Request

Backend:

{
 "users":[]
}

Gateway:

Return Response

API Gateway Is NOT

Many people confuse this.

API Gateway is NOT:

Database

❌

Application Server

❌

Container Runner

❌

Image Registry

❌

It is:

Traffic Entry Layer

Interview Question

What is API Gateway?

Good answer:

API Gateway is a managed AWS service that acts as a single entry point for APIs and routes requests to backend services while handling security, throttling, monitoring, and request management.

One sentence to remember

API Gateway receives requests. Backend processes requests.

Next:

1.2 Why API Gateway Exists (why not expose ECS/Lambda directly)

3. Why API Gateway Exists

Perfect. This is the section where API Gateway starts making sense.

1.2 Why API Gateway Exists

Question:

If users can already call ECS or Lambda directly… why add API Gateway?

Short answer:

Because exposing backends directly becomes difficult to secure, manage, scale, and standardize.

Problem Without API Gateway

Imagine:

Users
 ↓
ECS
 ↓
Container

Looks simple.

But now users know:

Server Address
Ports
Backend Structure

And every backend must implement:

Auth
Rate limits
Validation
Monitoring
Routing

Repeated everywhere.

Problem 1 — Too Many Entry Points

Imagine:

users-service
payments-service
courses-service
notifications-service

Without gateway:

users.company.com
payments.company.com
courses.company.com
notifications.company.com

Clients manage all URLs.

Mess.

With Gateway:

api.company.com

Routes:

/users
/payments
/courses

Single entry.

Problem 2 — Security

Without API Gateway:

User
↓
Backend

Backend must check:

JWT
Limits
Headers
Permissions

Every service.

With Gateway:

User
↓
API Gateway
↓
Backend

Gateway handles:

Auth
Rate limiting
Request filtering

Backend focuses on business logic.

Problem 3 — Rate Limiting

Imagine attacker:

100000 requests

Without gateway:

Containers overloaded

With gateway:

Limit:
100 req/sec

Gateway rejects.

Example:

429 Too Many Requests

before backend executes.

Problem 4 — Backend Changes

Current:

/users
↓
ECS

Tomorrow:

/users
↓
Lambda

Clients:

No changes

Because:

API Gateway stays same

Problem 5 — Monitoring

Without Gateway:

Need logs everywhere.

With Gateway:

You can see:

Requests
Latency
Errors
Traffic

in one place.

Problem 6 — Request Transformation

Client sends:

{
 "name":"Ali"
}

Gateway can transform.

Backend receives:

{
 "userName":"Ali"
}

Acts like middleware.

Browser
↓
ALB
↓
ECS
↓
Database

Simple.

With Gateway:

Browser
↓
API Gateway
↓
ALB
↓

↓
Database

Extra control layer.

Without Gateway:

Browser
↓
Lambda

Problem:

No public API layer

With Gateway:

↓

This is classic serverless.

Real Company Example

Company:

Mobile
Web
Admin

All call:

api.company.com

Gateway routes:

/login → Lambda
/users → ECS
/files → ECS

Backend hidden.

Compare With Yesterday's ALB

ALB:

Traffic Distribution

API Gateway:

API Management

ALB cares:

Where request goes

API Gateway cares:

Who
What
How many
Where

We will compare deeply later.

Interview Question

Why use API Gateway instead of exposing ECS directly?

Answer:

Because API Gateway centralizes routing, authentication, throttling, monitoring, and API management while hiding backend implementation.

One sentence to remember

API Gateway exists so clients talk to one controlled entrance instead of directly to backend services.

1.3 API Gateway vs Load Balancer

This one is extremely important because people confuse them constantly.

4.API GATEWAY VS LOAD BALANCER

Perfect. This is one of the most misunderstood AWS topics.

People often say:

“API Gateway is just Load Balancer.”

No.

They solve different problems.

1.3 API Gateway vs Load Balancer

Short answer:

Load Balancer distributes traffic.

API Gateway manages APIs.

First Look at Architecture

Load Balancer

Users
 ↓
ALB
 ↓
ECS
 ├── Container 1
 ├── Container 2
 └── Container 3

Question ALB answers:

Which backend instance should receive this request?

API Gateway

Users
 ↓
API Gateway
 ↓
Lambda / ALB / ECS

Question API Gateway answers:

Should request be allowed and where should it go?

Core Responsibility

API GatewayLoad Balancer
Main GoalManage APIsDistribute traffic
RoutingAPI routesBackend targets
AuthenticationYesLimited
Rate limitingYesNo
TransformationYesNo
VersioningYesNo
MonitoringAPI-focusedTraffic-focused
Backend abstractionStrongWeak
Lambda integrationNativeNo
ECS integrationYesYes

Mental Model

Load Balancer:

Traffic Controller

API Gateway:

Reception + Security + Controller

Example — ALB

Suppose:

3 ECS Tasks

Request:

GET /users

Flow:

ALB
↓
Choose Container
↓
Forward

Example:

Request 1 → Task 1
Request 2 → Task 2
Request 3 → Task 3

This is balancing.

Example — API Gateway

Request:

POST /payments

Flow:

Authenticate
↓
Validate
↓
Rate limit
↓
Route
↓
Backend

Different responsibility.

Without API Gateway:

Users
↓
ALB
↓
ECS
↓
Containers

Very common.

With API Gateway:

Users

API Gateway
↓
ALB
↓
ECS
↓
Containers

Gateway manages API.

Serverless Architecture

API Gateway:

Users
↓
API Gateway
↓
Lambda

No ALB.

Because Lambda auto-scales.

↓

Process request

Simple Analogy

Airport.

Security Gate

Checks:

Identity
Permission
Destination

Airport Staff

Chooses:

Which airplane

Performance Thinking

Huge traffic

API Gateway optimized for:

API control

When To Choose

Use ALB when:

Simple routing
High throughput

Use API Gateway when:

Public APIs
Auth
Rate limiting

API products

+
Need container balancing

↓

Interview Questions

Can API Gateway replace ALB?

Sometimes.

Example:

API Gateway
↓
Lambda

No ALB needed.

Can ALB replace API Gateway?

Partially.

Routing yes.

API management no.

Which comes first?

For API architectures usually:

Users
↓
API Gateway
↓

↓

API Gateway decides whether and where requests go. Load Balancer decides which backend instance gets them.

HTTP vs REST API in AWS

Perfect question.

This is specifically AWS API Gateway terminology, not generic REST vs HTTP protocol.

People confuse this.

In API Gateway:

  • REST API → older, more feature-rich gateway type
  • HTTP API → newer, simpler, cheaper, faster

REST API vs HTTP API (API Gateway)

FeatureREST APIHTTP API
ReleaseOlderNewer
CostHigherLower
PerformanceGoodFaster
ConfigurationMore complexSimpler
AuthenticationVery richSimpler
Request transformationStrongLimited
API KeysYesLimited
Usage PlansYesNo
CachingYesNo
Lambda IntegrationYesYes
ECS/ALB IntegrationYesYes
Recommended for new APIsSometimesUsually yes

First Understand They Are NOT Different Protocols

This is wrong:

REST → HTTP
HTTP API → TCP

No.

Both use:

HTTP

Difference is AWS feature set.

Simple
Cheap
Fast

↓

Response

↓

↓

Interview Question

Starting new project in API Gateway — which one?

Good answer:

Start with HTTP API unless you specifically need REST API features like API keys, usage plans, request transformations, or caching.

One sentence to remember

HTTP API = simpler and cheaper. REST API = richer and more configurable.

2.2 Resource

Question:

What is a Resource in API Gateway?

Short answer:

Resource represents a URL path inside your API.

Example:

/users
/courses
/invites
/payments

Each of these is a Resource.

First Understand Resource Concept

Imagine your CRM.

You expose:

GET /users
POST /users

GET /courses
POST /courses

GET /invites

Resources are:

/users
/courses
/invites

Methods are separate.

Resource ≠ Method

People confuse this.

Wrong:

GET /users
=
Resource

No.

Correct:

/users
=
Resource
GET
POST
DELETE
=
Methods

Visual:

Resource
/users
   ├── GET
   ├── POST
   └── DELETE

Resource = Noun

Usually resources represent entities.

Examples:

/users
/courses
/students
/orders

Good.

Bad:

/getUsers
/createUser

Because methods already describe action.

Resource Hierarchy

Resources can be nested.

Example:

/courses
/courses/{id}
/courses/{id}/lessons

Hierarchy:

/courses
 └── /{id}
      └── /lessons

School API

Resource

 }

Create new

PUT

Replace data.

DELETE

Does Gateway talk directly to ECS?

Usually through ALB.

Can Gateway invoke Lambda?

Yes.

Can Gateway work without backend?

With AWS service integrations sometimes yes.

One sentence to remember

Integration determines who actually performs the work after API Gateway receives the request.

1.1 What is Lambda?

Lambda is an AWS service that lets you run code without managing servers.

Short definition:

Upload code → AWS executes it when an event happens.

You do NOT manage:

EC2
OS
Scaling
Containers
Servers

You manage:

Code
Memory
Timeout
Config

Core Idea

Traditional:

User
↓
Server
↓
Application
↓
Response

Server always exists.

Lambda:

Event
↓
Lambda
↓
Run Code
↓
Response
↓
Stop

No always-running server.

Example 1 — API

Browser
↓
API Gateway
↓
Lambda
↓
Database

Request:

POST /login

↓

Lambda runs:

handler()

↓

Returns.

Example 2 — File Upload

S3 Upload
↓
Lambda
↓
Resize Image

No API.

Example 3 — Queue Processing

SQS
↓
Lambda
↓
Send Email

Lambda Unit = Function

Example:

export const handler = async () => {
 return {
   statusCode:200
 }
}

AWS runs:

handler()

Compare To ECS

ECS:

Container
always available

Lambda:

Execute
↓
Finish
↓
Sleep

Compare To EC2

EC2:

You manage server

Lambda:

AWS manages server

Real Flow

Trigger
↓
Lambda
↓
Execute
↓
Return
↓
Destroy / Freeze

Architecture Position

Users
↓
API Gateway
↓
Lambda
↓
Database

or

S3
↓
Lambda
↓
Process

Interview Answer

Lambda is a serverless compute service that executes code in response to events without requiring server management.

One sentence to remember

Lambda runs code only when triggered.

why Lambda

1.2 Why Lambda Exists

Question:

If EC2 and ECS already run applications… why did AWS create Lambda?

Short answer:

Because many workloads do not need always-running servers.

Problem Without Lambda

Imagine login endpoint.

Traffic:

09:00 → 1000 req
09:05 → 0 req

EC2:

Server still running

ECS:

Container still running

You still pay.

Lambda:

Request
↓
Execute
↓
Stop

Pay only when code runs.

Problem 1 — Servers Stay Idle

Traditional:

EC2
↓
24/7

Even if:

No traffic

Lambda:

No event
↓
No execution
↓
No compute cost

Problem 2 — Autoscaling Complexity

Without Lambda:

Traffic ↑
↓
Add Servers
↓
Load Balancer
↓
Scaling Rules

Complex.

Lambda:

Traffic ↑
↓
More executions

AWS handles scaling.

Problem 3 — Event-Based Work

Example:

Upload image.

Traditional:

Server
↓
Wait
↓
Wait
↓
Wait

Waste.

Lambda:

S3 Upload
↓
Trigger
↓
Resize
↓
Stop

Only runs when needed.

Problem 4 — Small APIs

Example:

/login
/contact
/send-email

Running ECS for this can be too much.

Lambda:

Request
↓
Function
↓
Return

Simple.

Real Example

Password reset.

Flow:

User clicks
↓
API Gateway
↓
Lambda
↓
Send Email
↓
Done

No container.

Compare To ECS

ECS:

Container
running

Lambda:

Execution
only when needed

Compare To EC2

EC2:

Manage servers
Patch
Scale

Lambda:

Upload code
AWS runs

When Lambda Is Great

APIs
Events
Automation
Queues
Image processing
Notifications

When Lambda Is Bad

Long-running services
WebSockets
Heavy containers
Large state

(Generally ECS fits better.)

Rent house

ECS:

Rent apartment

Lambda:

Call taxi

Use → leave.

2.6 Stateless Execution

Most important Lambda concept.

Lambda should not depend on memory.

Bad:

execution 1
↓
save memory
↓

Good:

Request
↓
DB
↓
Response

Every execution should work independently.

Store state in:

RDS
Redis
S3
DynamoDB

Not memory.

SYSTEM_DESIGN
6.5.20206-System Design(Layered Architecture, DDD(domain driven design), Clean Architecture)
Layered Architecture
Overal

1. Overall

Layered Architecture is a software architecture style where the application is divided into separate layers, and each layer has a specific responsibility.

The most common layers are:

Client / Browser
     ↓
Presentation Layer
     ↓
Business Layer
     ↓
Data Access Layer
     ↓
Database

Example:

HTTP Request
   ↓
Controller
   ↓
Service
   ↓
Repository
   ↓
Database

In backend development, this is one of the most common beginner-to-enterprise architectures.

Project Structure

Example NestJS layered structure:

src/
├── modules/
│   └── courses/
│       ├── controllers/
│       │   └── courses.controller.ts
│       │
│       ├── services/
│       │   └── courses.service.ts
│       │
│       ├── repositories/
│       │   └── courses.repository.ts
│       │
│       ├── dto/
│       │   ├── create-course.dto.ts
│       │   └── course-response.dto.ts
│       │
│       ├── entities/
│       │   └── course.entity.ts
│       │
│       └── courses.module.ts
│
├── shared/
│   ├── decorators/
│   ├── guards/
│   └── exceptions/
│
└── main.ts

Responsibility of Each Folder

FolderResponsibility
controllers/Handles HTTP requests/responses
services/Contains business logic
repositories/Talks to database
dto/Defines request/response shape
entities/Represents database/domain objects
shared/Common reusable code
structural analysis (what for why)

Controller

What?

Controller is the entry point of HTTP requests.

@Controller('courses')
exportclassCoursesController {
  constructor(privatereadonlycoursesService:CoursesService) {}

@Post()
async create(@Body()body:CreateCourseDto) {
returnthis.coursesService.createCourse(body);
  }
}

For what?

Used for:

  • receiving request
  • reading params/body/query
  • calling service
  • returning response

Why?

Because HTTP logic should not be mixed with business logic.

Controller should know about:

HTTP, request, response, status codes, decorators

Controller should NOT contain heavy business rules.

Service

What?

Service contains application/business logic.

@Injectable()
exportclassCoursesService {
  constructor(privatereadonlycoursesRepository:CoursesRepository) {}

async createCourse(input:CreateCourseDto) {
if (!input.title) {
thrownewBadRequestException('Title is required');
    }

returnthis.coursesRepository.create(input);
  }
}

For what?

Used for:

  • business decisions
  • validation logic
  • orchestration
  • calling repositories
  • coordinating multiple operations

Why?

Because business rules should be separated from HTTP and database code.

Repository

What?

Repository is responsible for database communication.

@Injectable()
exportclassCoursesRepository {
async create(data:CreateCourseDto) {
returndb.course.create({ data });
  }

async findById(id:string) {
returndb.course.findUnique({ where: { id } });
  }
}

For what?

Used for:

  • queries
  • insert/update/delete
  • database abstraction

Why?

Because service should not directly depend on raw database queries everywhere.

Bad:

// service directly talks to DB
awaitdb.course.create(...)

Better:

awaitthis.coursesRepository.create(...)

Entity / Model

What?

Represents a data object.

exportclassCourse {
  id:string;
  title:string;
  description:string;
  state:'draft'|'published';
  creatorId:string;
}

For what?

Used to describe structure of application data.

Why?

Because the app needs a consistent model of important objects.

DTO

What?

DTO means Data Transfer Object.

exportclassCreateCourseDto {
  title:string;
  description:string;
}

For what?

Used for request and response shape.

Why?

Because database entity and API response should not always be the same.

Example:

Database entity:

{
id,
title,
password,
deletedAt,
createdAt
}

Response DTO:

{
id,
title,
createdAt
}

You should not expose everything.

when to use

Use it when:

  • app is small or medium size
  • business logic is not extremely complex
  • team needs simple structure
  • CRUD operations are dominant
  • you are building admin panels, dashboards, APIs
  • project does not need heavy domain modeling yet

Example projects:

CRM
LMS
POS system
Blog API
Admin dashboard
Inventory system

For your LMS or POS project, layered architecture is a good starting point.

pros and cons

Pros

ProsExplanation
SimpleEasy to understand
CommonUsed in many companies
Beginner friendlyClear controller-service-repository flow
TestableYou can test services separately
OrganizedCode has clear locations
Good for CRUDWorks well for database-heavy apps

Cons

ConsExplanation
Business logic leakageLogic may spread between layers
Fat servicesServices become too large
Weak domain modelEntities become just data containers
Hard scalingLarge projects become messy
Too much couplingService may know too much
Framework dependencyCode often depends heavily on NestJS/Spring/etc.
Request flow inside layered architecture

Example request:

POST /courses

Flow:

Client
  ↓
Controller
  ↓
Service
  ↓
Repository
  ↓
Database
  ↓
Repository
  ↓
Service
  ↓
Controller
  ↓
Client

Code example:

// controller
@Post()
create(@Body()body:CreateCourseDto) {
returnthis.coursesService.createCourse(body);
}
// service
asynccreateCourse(input:CreateCourseDto) {
returnthis.coursesRepository.create(input);
}
// repository
asynccreate(data:CreateCourseDto) {
returnthis.prisma.course.create({ data });
}
Dependency direction between layers

Correct direction:

Controller → Service → Repository → Database

Meaning:

  • controller depends on service
  • service depends on repository
  • repository depends on database

Bad direction:

Repository → Service
Service → Controller

Repository should never call service.

Controller should never be used inside service.

Separation of concerns

Each layer has one main concern.

LayerConcern
ControllerHTTP
ServiceBusiness logic
RepositoryDatabase
DTOInput/output shape
EntityData representation

Bad example:

@Post()
asynccreate(@Body()body) {
if (body.title.length<3) {
thrownewError();
  }

returndb.course.create({ data:body });
}

Problem:

Controller is doing:

  • validation
  • business logic
  • database operation

Better:

@Post()
create(@Body()body:CreateCourseDto) {
returnthis.coursesService.createCourse(body);
}
Coupling vs cohesion in layered systems

Coupling

Coupling means how much one part depends on another.

Bad coupling:

CoursesService directly uses Prisma everywhere
awaitthis.prisma.course.create(...)

Better:

awaitthis.coursesRepository.create(...)

Now service does not care exactly how database works.

Cohesion

Cohesion means related code stays together.

Good cohesion:

courses/
├── courses.controller.ts
├── courses.service.ts
├── courses.repository.ts

Bad cohesion:

controllers/courses.controller.ts
services/courses.service.ts
repositories/courses.repository.ts

Feature-based structure is usually better for larger apps.

Common layers explanation

Presentation Layer

Responsible for external communication.

Example:

@Controller('courses')
exportclassCoursesController {}

Includes:

  • controllers
  • routes
  • request parsing
  • response formatting

Business Layer

Responsible for application rules.

Example:

asyncpublishCourse(courseId:string,userId:string) {
constcourse=awaitthis.repository.findById(courseId);

if (!course) {
thrownewNotFoundException();
  }

if (course.creatorId!==userId) {
thrownewForbiddenException();
  }

returnthis.repository.update(courseId, { state:'published' });
}

Data Access Layer

Responsible for database access.

Example:

asyncfindById(id:string) {
returnthis.prisma.course.findUnique({
    where: { id },
  });
}

Database Layer

Actual persistence system.

Examples:

PostgreSQL
MySQL
MongoDB
Redis
DynamoDB
Presentation

Example: Create Course API

Controller

@Post()
@Roles('instructor','admin')
asynccreate(@Body()body:CreateCourseDto,@CurrentUser()user:User) {
returnthis.coursesService.createCourse(user.id,body);
}

Service

asynccreateCourse(creatorId:string,input:CreateCourseDto) {
if (!input.title||input.title.length<3) {
thrownewBadRequestException('Title is too short');
  }

returnthis.coursesRepository.create({
    title:input.title,
    description:input.description,
    creatorId,
    state:'draft',
  });
}

Repository

asynccreate(data:CreateCourseData) {
returnthis.prisma.course.create({
    data,
  });
}

Flow:

Controller receives HTTP
Service applies rules
Repository saves data
Database stores course

asynccreateCourse(creatorId:string,input:CreateCourseDto) {
if (!input.title||input.title.length<3) {

returnthis.coursesRepository.create({

Repository

asynccreate(data:CreateCourseData) {

Service applies rules

Typical mistakes

Mistake 1: Business logic in controller

Bad:

@Post()
asynccreate(@Body()body) {
if (body.price<0) {
thrownewError();
  }

returnthis.repository.create(body);
}

Mistake 2: Repository contains business logic

Bad:

asyncpublishCourse(id:string,user:User) {
if (user.role!=='admin') {
thrownewError();
  }

returndb.course.update(...)
}

Repository should not decide business rules.

Mistake 3: Service becomes too big

Bad:

courses.service.ts
- createCourse()
- updateCourse()
- publishCourse()
- enrollStudent()
- calculateProgress()
- issueCertificate()
- sendEmail()
- uploadFile()

This becomes a fat service.

Layer leakage problem

Layer leakage means one layer starts doing another layer’s job.

Example:

// controller knows database details
returnthis.prisma.course.findMany();

Problem:

Controller is leaking into data access layer.

Another example:

// repository checks business role
if (user.role!=='admin')thrownewError();

Repository is leaking into business layer.

Correct:

Controller → HTTP only
Service → business rules
Repository → DB only
Fat service problem

A fat service is a service class with too many responsibilities.

Example:

CoursesService
├── createCourse()
├── updateCourse()
├── publishCourse()
├── archiveCourse()
├── enrollStudent()
├── calculateProgress()
├── sendNotification()
├── generateCertificate()
└── uploadThumbnail()

Problem:

The service becomes a mini-monolith.

Solution:

Split by use case:

courses/
├── services/
│   ├── create-course.service.ts
│   ├── publish-course.service.ts
│   ├── enroll-student.service.ts
│   └── archive-course.service.ts

Or move toward Clean Architecture use cases later.

Anemic business logic problem

Anemic model means entities only hold data and have no behavior.

Example:

classCourse {
  id:string;
  title:string;
  state:string;
}

Then all logic is outside:

if (course.state==='draft') {
course.state='published';
}

Problem:

Business rules are not protected.

DDD prefers:

classCourse {
  publish() {
if (this.state!=='draft') {
thrownewError('Only draft courses can be published');
    }

this.state='published';
  }
}

Layered architecture often causes anemic models because logic lives in services.

Scalability limitations

Layered architecture can scale technically, but structurally it may become difficult.

Problems in large systems:

Huge services
Too many dependencies
Business logic duplication
Repository methods exploding
Hard testing
Hard refactoring

Example:

users.service.ts
courses.service.ts
payments.service.ts
notifications.service.ts
reports.service.ts

At scale, services start calling each other too much.

Example:

CoursesService → UsersService → PaymentsService → NotificationsService

This creates tight coupling.

Testing approach

Controller Test

Tests HTTP layer.

Example:

Does POST /courses return 201?
Does invalid body return 400?

Service Test

Tests business logic.

Example:

Should not publish course if user is not instructor
Should create draft course

Repository Test

Tests database queries.

Example:

Should insert course into database
Should find course by ID

Best testing target:

Service layer

Because most logic should be there.

Relation to monolith architecture

Layered architecture is very common in monoliths.

Example:

Monolith App
├── users
├── courses
├── payments
└── notifications

All modules exist in one application, but internally they use layers.

Controller → Service → Repository

Layered architecture does NOT mean monolith only.

But most monoliths use layered structure.

Relation to MVC

MVC:

Model
View
Controller

Layered backend:

Controller
Service
Repository
Database

MVC is more common in web apps with views.

Layered architecture is more common in APIs.

Comparison:

MVCLayered Architecture
ControllerController
ModelEntity/Repository
ViewFrontend/Template
ServiceOften added separately

Example Django:

views.py → service.py → models.py → database
Comparison with:

Layered vs Clean Architecture

LayeredClean Architecture
Framework-centeredDomain/use-case centered
Controller → Service → RepoDependency points inward
EasierMore flexible
Good for CRUDGood for complex business logic

Layered vs Hexagonal

LayeredHexagonal
Vertical layersCore + ports/adapters
Repository is lower layerRepository is adapter
DB often influences designDomain is protected

Layered vs DDD

LayeredDDD
Technical organizationBusiness/domain modeling
Service-heavyEntity/Aggregate behavior
CRUD-friendlyComplex business-friendly
Enterprise usage examples

Many enterprise systems use layered architecture:

Banking admin systems
ERP systems
CRM systems
LMS systems
Internal dashboards
Government systems
Insurance systems
Inventory systems

Example enterprise flow:

Admin creates customer
  ↓
CustomerController
  ↓
CustomerService
  ↓
CustomerRepository
  ↓
PostgreSQL

Why enterprises use it:

  • predictable
  • easy to onboard developers
  • works well with Java/Spring, NestJS, .NET
  • easy to test
  • easy to document
Folder/module organization strategies

Strategy 1: Layer-based folders

src/
├── controllers/
│   ├── courses.controller.ts
│   └── users.controller.ts
├── services/
│   ├── courses.service.ts
│   └── users.service.ts
├── repositories/
│   ├── courses.repository.ts
│   └── users.repository.ts
└── entities/
    ├── course.entity.ts
    └── user.entity.ts

Good for small apps.

Bad for large apps because related files are far apart.

Strategy 2: Feature-based folders

src/
├── courses/
│   ├── courses.controller.ts
│   ├── courses.service.ts
│   ├── courses.repository.ts
│   └── course.entity.ts
│
├── users/
│   ├── users.controller.ts
│   ├── users.service.ts
│   ├── users.repository.ts
│   └── user.entity.ts

Better for medium/large apps.

Strategy 3: Module + internal layers

src/
├── modules/
│   ├── courses/
│   │   ├── controllers/
│   │   ├── services/
│   │   ├── repositories/
│   │   ├── dto/
│   │   └── entities/
│   │
│   └── users/
│       ├── controllers/
│       ├── services/
│       ├── repositories/
│       ├── dto/
│       └── entities/

This is usually best for NestJS.

Transaction handling

Transaction means multiple DB operations succeed or fail together.

Example:

Create order
Decrease product stock
Create payment record

All must succeed together.

Bad:

awaitorderRepository.create(order);
awaitproductRepository.decreaseStock(productId);
awaitpaymentRepository.create(payment);

If payment fails, order may still be created.

Better:

awaitdb.transaction(async (tx) => {
awaitorderRepository.create(order,tx);
awaitproductRepository.decreaseStock(productId,tx);
awaitpaymentRepository.create(payment,tx);
});

Where to handle transaction?

Usually:

Service layer

Because service coordinates the use case.

Validation placement

There are different types of validation.

DTO validation

Basic input validation.

Example:

exportclassCreateCourseDto {
@IsString()
@MinLength(3)
  title:string;
}

Placed in:

DTO / Controller boundary

Business validation

Example:

Only draft course can be published
Only instructor can create course
Course limit cannot exceed 100 lessons

Placed in:

Service layer

or in DDD:

Domain entity / aggregate

Database validation

Example:

unique email
foreign key constraint
not null

Placed in:

Database schema
Authentication/authorization placement

Authentication

Authentication means:

Who are you?

Usually handled before controller using middleware/guard.

Example:

@UseGuards(AuthGuard)

Authorization

Authorization means:

What are you allowed to do?

Can be handled in:

Guard + Service

Example:

@Roles('admin','instructor')

But deeper ownership check belongs in service:

if (course.creatorId!==user.id) {
thrownewForbiddenException();
}

Because this is business-specific authorization.

DTO flow between layers

Common flow:

Request DTO
   ↓
Controller
   ↓
Service input
   ↓
Repository data
   ↓
Entity
   ↓
Response DTO

Example:

// Request DTO
{
title:"AWS Course",
description:"Learn AWS"
}

Service converts:

{
title,
description,
creatorId:user.id,
state:"draft"
}

Response DTO:

{
id,
title,
description,
state,
createdAt
}

Do not return raw database object if it contains sensitive fields.

Anti-patterns

1. God Service

One service does everything.

AppService
├── users
├── courses
├── payments
├── emails
└── reports

2. Controller with business logic

Controller becomes too smart.

3. Repository with business logic

Repository decides business rules.

4. Entity used as request DTO

Bad:

create(@Body() body: UserEntity)

Use DTO instead.

5. Service directly exposes database errors

Bad:

Prisma unique constraint error shown to user

Better:

Email already exists

6. Circular dependencies

Example:

CoursesService depends on UsersService
UsersService depends on CoursesService

Dangerous design smell.

When NOT to use layered architecture

Avoid pure layered architecture when:

  • business rules are very complex
  • domain has many invariants
  • project requires long-term maintainability
  • many teams work on different domains
  • microservices are based on business boundaries
  • you need strong independence from frameworks/database
  • you want use-case-driven design

Example:

Banking core system
Trading platform
Complex logistics system
Large LMS with many business workflows

In those cases, DDD + Clean Architecture may be better.

Migration problems from layered → clean/DDD architectures

Common problems:

1. Business logic already scattered

Logic exists in:

controllers
services
repositories
validators
database triggers

Hard to extract.

2. Services are too large

Example:

courses.service.ts = 1500 lines

Hard to split into use cases.

3. Entities are anemic

Entities only have data, no behavior.

DDD migration needs behavior moved into domain models.

4. Framework dependency everywhere

Example:

thrownewBadRequestException()

inside deep business logic.

Clean Architecture prefers domain errors independent from NestJS.

5. Repository interfaces missing

Service directly depends on Prisma/Sequelize.

Migration requires interfaces:

interfaceCoursesRepository {
  findById(id:string):Promise<Course>;
  save(course:Course):Promise<void>;
}

Final Mental Model

Layered Architecture is:

Simple technical separation of backend responsibilities.

Main flow:

Controller → Service → Repository → Database

Best for:

CRUD apps, admin panels, LMS, CRM, POS, dashboards

Main danger:

Business logic becomes scattered or service layer becomes too fat.

Best next step after understanding this:

DDD explains how to model business logic better.
Clean Architecture explains how to protect business logic from frameworks and databases.
